articles.title: Transportation secretary Sean Duffy flies $148K Jetson ONE at NASA
articles.excerpt: Sean Duffy flew a $148,000 Jetson ONE solo over NASA's Kennedy Space Center, and two days later five eVTOLs flew…
articles.fullText:
Seeing a $148,000 flying machine lift off at NASA's Kennedy Space Center would be impressive on its own. Now put U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy in the pilot's seat. That's exactly what happened recently when Duffy took a Jetson ONE for a solo flight over the Florida spaceport. Two days later, five of these personal electric aircraft were flying in formation during a public airshow.
Jetson says Duffy became the first sitting U.S. transportation secretary to pilot a personal electric vertical takeoff and landing aircraft, better known as an eVTOL. His flight also raises an interesting question about where personal aviation is heading. After all, we're talking about an aircraft that can fly without its operator needing a pilot's license under certain FAA rules. But before you start clearing space in your garage, let's look at what this aircraft can actually do and where you can legally fly it.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.
Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
AIR TAXIS CUT HOUR-LONG COMMUTES TO MINUTES, RIDERS MAY BE SHOCKED BY THE PRICE
Duffy climbed into the single-seat Jetson ONE during the UP.Summit gathering at Kennedy Space Center. He lifted off vertically and performed flybys using the aircraft's joystick controls. Jetson says its computerized flight system automatically helps stabilize the aircraft, making it easier to maneuver.
After landing, Duffy made his enthusiasm clear. "Personal flight isn't the future anymore, it's here," he said.
For Jetson, having the nation's top transportation official experience the aircraft firsthand was a major moment. However, Duffy's flight did not change any FAA regulations or expand where the Jetson ONE can legally operate.
Duffy's solo flight was only part of the excitement. During the November MAX POWER airshow, Jetson sent five aircraft into a synchronized formation from Kennedy Space Center's historic Shuttle Landing Facility. The event also featured NASA research aircraft and the U.S. Air Force Thunderbirds.
Among the five Jetson aircraft was Astro, the flying police vehicle owned by the Florida Polytechnic University Police Department. We recently covered this $148,000 electric police aircraft , which the university hopes to use for public safety operations.
Astro features police lights and a special registration, N911FP. At Kennedy Space Center, the aircraft took part in the formation flight and appeared on display for attendees. However, its participation in the airshow does not establish that the department has received approval for routine police operations. The university has been pursuing separate FAA authorization.
FLYING SPORTS CAR HIDES ITS WINGS AS PRODUCTION GETS CLOSER
The Jetson ONE looks like a giant drone with a seat in the middle. Eight electric motors power its propellers, allowing it to take off vertically without a runway. The aircraft also has an open cockpit and a lightweight aluminum frame that folds for storage. According to Jetson's published specifications, the aircraft can reach 63 mph and stay airborne for approximately 20 minutes per charge. It carries one person, with a maximum pilot weight of 210 pounds.
Jetson also highlights several safety features, including a ballistic parachute and radar-assisted automatic landing. The company says the aircraft can remain airborne if one motor fails. Those features sound reassuring, although they cannot eliminate the risks of flying.
Then there's the price. A Jetson ONE currently costs $148,000 before taxes and additional fees. Jetson says its 2026 and 2027 production slots are already sold out, with new orders targeting 2028 delivery. So even if you're ready to spend the money, you won't be taking delivery anytime soon.
Here's something that might surprise you. Jetson designed the ONE to operate under the FAA's Part 103 ultralight regulations. Qualifying aircraft can be flown recreationally without a pilot's license or an airworthiness certificate.
But the rules come with restrictions. Under FAA Part 103 regulations, ultralights are limited to recreational or sporting purposes. Operators generally must fly during daylight hours and cannot fly over congested cities or outdoor gatherings. Flights in certain controlled airspace also require prior authorization.
Weight is another important factor. Jetson lists the ONE at 253 pounds with batteries. That's just below the 254-pound empty-weight limit for powered ultralights under Part 103. The FAA also applies specific rules to how that weight is calculated. These regulations help explain why the Florida Polytechnic University Police Department needs separate FAA authorization before using Astro for official law enforcement operations.
Jetson previously said the university required approval under Part 91 to integrate the aircraft into police work. That's also why Duffy's flight deserves attention. He oversees the department responsible for the FAA, and he's now experienced this technology himself. Whether that leads to new discussions about personal electric aircraft remains to be seen.
Duffy isn't the only prominent figure showing interest in Jetson. On Nov. 2, the company announced that Sir Peter Beck, founder and CEO of Rocket Lab, had become a Jetson ONE owner after experiencing the aircraft firsthand. According to Jetson's announcement, Beck has already received his Founders Edition aircraft.
The company expects it to fly by Christmas, pending regulatory approvals. Having a rocket company founder purchase one certainly gives Jetson another high-profile supporter. However, we'll learn much more as additional aircraft reach customers and begin flying outside carefully organized demonstrations.
You probably won't see a Jetson ONE flying over your neighborhood anytime soon. Its $148,000 price puts it well beyond most people's budgets, and the roughly 20-minute flight time limits how far it can practically travel.
FAA restrictions also prevent recreational ultralights from flying over congested areas. Still, it's exciting to see personal electric aircraft moving into customers' hands. And with police departments exploring the technology, there could eventually be applications beyond recreational flying.
If you're considering buying one, take the training seriously, even though qualifying Part 103 ultralights don't require a pilot's license. You'll also want to understand exactly where you can legally fly before making such a large purchase.
I have to admit, I'd love to take a Jetson ONE for a spin. The idea of lifting off vertically and flying around in something this compact sounds like an incredible experience. Seeing five of them together at Kennedy Space Center makes me even more curious about where this technology could go. But I also have questions about how we're going to handle more personal aircraft sharing our skies.
Duffy has now experienced one firsthand, and I hope that leads to some serious conversations about safety and how these aircraft should be regulated. I'm especially interested in what happens with Florida Polytechnic's flying police vehicle. That's where we'll start to see whether this technology can deliver something useful beyond recreational flying.
Would you trust yourself to fly a Jetson ONE without a pilot's license, or should the FAA require formal training before anyone takes one into the sky? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com

articles.title: App breach may expose 500,000 construction workers
articles.excerpt: The personal data of some 500,000 registered construction workers was potentially exposed on Saturday after unauthorized access was discovered on…
articles.fullText:
The personal data of some 500,000 registered construction workers was potentially exposed on Saturday after unauthorized access was discovered on the Construction Industry Council (CIC) app server.

The information that may have been accessed includes names, dates of birth and ID numbers, though no financial data was involved.

The CIC app is used by workers for registration, attendance checks as well as job searches.

The council has suspended the app's operation and reported the incident to the police.

It said it has called in a third-party cybersecurity forensics expert and notified the Office of the Privacy Commissioner for Personal Data as well as the Digital Policy Office.

It apologised for the incident, vowing to continue strengthening its cybersecurity measures and adding that it would notify affected workers as soon as possible.

Edited by Azam Khan

articles.title: All systems go: mainland ready for Shenzhou-23 return
articles.excerpt: The astronauts from the Shenzhou-23 and Shenzhou-24 missions on Saturday completed their in-orbit handover at the nation's Tiangong Space Station…
articles.fullText:
The astronauts from the Shenzhou-23 and Shenzhou-24 missions on Saturday completed their in-orbit handover at the nation's Tiangong Space Station.

Those returning are two Shenzhou-23 astronauts, Zhang Zhiyuan, the SAR's Lai Ka-ying, together with Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali from the Shenzhou-24 mission.

Back on earth, mainland authorities said the Dongfeng landing site completed its final safety drill ahead of Shenzhou-23's return in the coming days.

The drill simulated key mission procedures, including aerial search and rescue and ground handling, while testing the technical status of equipment such as measurement and communication devices.

Meanwhile, Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and army chief Syed Asim Munir held a space-ground call with Pakistan's first-ever astronaut Ali on Saturday.

According to the China Manned Space Agency, Sharif and Munir were at the headquarters of the Pakistan Space and Upper Atmosphere Research Commission for the call with Ali, the first foreign astronaut to board Tiangong. (With contributions from Xinhua)

Edited by Azam Khan

articles.title: Europe keen to learn from HK digital finance policies
articles.excerpt: The European Union is keen to learn from Hong Kong's policies and regulations on tokenisation, Secretary for Financial Services and…
articles.fullText:
The European Union is keen to learn from Hong Kong's policies and regulations on tokenisation, Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury Christopher Hui said following his four-day trip to Germany, Belgium and Luxembourg.

Speaking on a Commercial Radio programme on Saturday, he said the bloc had expressed great interest in the city's capital market and green finance development, as well as its connectivity with the mainland.

"They hope to learn from us to some extent, and then see whether they can use similar measures at home to drive their own development," Hui said.

Finance officials from Belgium and Luxembourg were, he added, keen to study the city's latest financial initiatives, such as its digital green bonds.

Back in 2023, Hong Kong was among the first few governments to have issued tokenised green bond.

Earlier this year, it set a record for the world's largest digital bond issuance, worth around HK$20 billion.

Hui said a European think tank he met had begun researching the internationalisation of the yuan as it looked at how the region's firms could get more involved in the development of China and Asia.

"Europe in particular has a very strong interest in Asia," he said.

"At the same time, they really want to know what advice or methods Hong Kong has to help them take a bigger part in that development."

Edited by Azam Khan

articles.title: 200 flee building scaffolding fire in Tuen Mun
articles.excerpt: A scaffolding net caught fire on the exterior wall of an industrial building in Tuen Mun on Saturday afternoon, forcing…
articles.fullText:
A scaffolding net caught fire on the exterior wall of an industrial building in Tuen Mun on Saturday afternoon, forcing about 200 people to evacuate.

The Fire Services Department said the blaze started at around 2pm at the building on Kin Fat Lane and classified it as a No 1 alarm fire.

One jet and one breathing apparatus team were sent to fight the fire, which has since been largely extinguished.

No injuries have been reported so far.

The incident occurred on a day when the Observatory had issued the red fire danger warning, indicating extreme risks.

Edited by Azam Khan

articles.title: OpenAI countersues Apple as partnership gets uglier
articles.excerpt: OpenAI is suing Apple, accusing the tech giant of stealing its trade secrets and discouraging hardware suppliers from working on…
articles.fullText:
OpenAI is suing Apple, accusing the tech giant of stealing its trade secrets and discouraging hardware suppliers from working on its planned devices, after Apple sued OpenAI for allegedly poaching its employees to gain access to its technology.

It filed counterclaims in California federal court on Friday, saying that Apple's employment practices were designed to "trap" employees and prevent them from working on competitors' technology.

OpenAI, whose ChatGPT is integrated into some generations of iPhones, is developing AI-enabled personal electronic devices that threaten to "outcompete Apple on what Apple views as its own turf", the company said in its Friday court filing.

OpenAI said in the filing that Apple gained confidential information by rehiring a former employee who worked at OpenAI for six months. In that time, the employee gained access to specific information on a new device as well as OpenAI's roadmap for future hardware products.

"Given the timing, it now appears that stealing those documents may have been his reason for joining OpenAI in the first place," it said.

Apple denied using the rehired employee to access OpenAI's confidential information and denied trying to suppress competition in AI device manufacturing.

"OpenAI’s counterclaims are a transparent attempt to distract from the substance of Apple’s lawsuit," Apple said.

Tensions between the two tech companies have escalated as the intensifying race to develop AI products fuels competition for talent and proprietary technology.

Apple sued OpenAI and former Apple employees Tang Tan and Chang Liu in July, alleging misappropriation of its trade secrets to benefit the ChatGPT owner's foray into consumer hardware.

Tan, a 24-year Apple employee who had been a vice president of product design for iPhone and Apple Watch, was part of the group that launched the AI device startup io Products before it was acquired by OpenAI in 2025.

OpenAI and the employees have denied those allegations and said that Apple's lawsuit depended on its unauthorized monitoring of Liu's personal messages after he stopped working for Apple.

In Friday's filing, OpenAI criticised Apple for encouraging employees to do work on their personal Apple devices and accounts, then preventing those employees from an orderly separation of work and personal accounts when they leave for new jobs.

OpenAI said that Apple continues to access former employees' personal devices and accounts after they leave the company, enabling Apple to "monitor and ensnare departing employees" when they leave for competitors.

OpenAI said that 400 employees have left Apple for OpenAI so far, and Apple wants to intimidate other employees from leaving to find other tech companies. (Reuters)

Edited by Azam Khan

articles.title: Gold Medal for Bravery for fallen firefighter
articles.excerpt: Senior fireman Ho Wai-ho, who died in the Wang Fuk Court blaze last November, was awarded the Gold Medal for…
articles.fullText:
Senior fireman Ho Wai-ho, who died in the Wang Fuk Court blaze last November, was awarded the Gold Medal for Bravery as Chief Executive John Lee presented this year's honours at Government House on Saturday.

Ho's brother and fiancée accepted the award as the room applauded for about half a minute.

The ceremony comes just two days after the one-year anniversary of the deadly Tai Po blaze that claimed 168 lives.

Three people received the Grand Bauhinia Medal, the city's highest honour, including Executive Council member and incoming Hospital Authority chairman Chan Kin-por, economist Lawrence Lau and banker Lam Kwong-siu.

Eight people were awarded the Gold Bauhinia Star, including lawmaker Gary Chan, Chinese University vice-chancellor Dennis Lo and outgoing Hospital Authority chairman Henry Fan.

Nineteen people received the Silver Bauhinia Star while 40 received the Bronze Bauhinia Star.

A total of 466 people, 39 more than last year, are being recognised at this year's presentation ceremony which runs across Saturday and Sunday.

Edited by Azam Khan

articles.title: Italy make Davis Cup final as Musetti aces his matches
articles.excerpt: Singles and doubles wins by Lorenzo Musetti allowed defending champion Italy to edge the Czech Republic 2-1 in a Davis…
articles.fullText:
Singles and doubles wins by Lorenzo Musetti allowed defending champion Italy to edge the Czech Republic 2-1 in a Davis Cup finals semifinal match in Bologna, Italy.

The series was decided in the third match on Friday, when the Italian pair of Musetti and Andrea Vavassori rallied past Jiri Lehecka and Tomas Machac 3-6, 6-1, 7-6 (4).

Neither side broke serve in the third set, and the tiebreaker was level 4-4 before the Italians reeled off the final three points.

"We put more heart on court," Italy captain Filippo Volandri said, according to the Davis Cup website. "We were ready to die on court."

Musetti gave Italy the early advantage with a 6-3, 6-4 victory over the Czech Republic's Jakub Mensik. Lehecka pulled the Czechs even by defeating Italy's Flavio Cobolli 6-2, 1-6, 6-3.

Great Britain and Spain will meet in the second semifinal on Saturday, with the winner facing Italy on Sunday. Italy can become the first country to win four consecutive Davis Cup titles since the United States in 1971. (Reuters)

Edited by Azam Khan

articles.title: Tech networking 'key in Hung Shui Kiu university race'
articles.excerpt: Secretary for Education Christine Choi said she hopes the university town in Hung Shui Kiu will foster collaboration across disciplines…
articles.fullText:
Secretary for Education Christine Choi said she hopes the university town in Hung Shui Kiu will foster collaboration across disciplines, industries and institutions.

Speaking on a television programme on Saturday, she said institutions bringing courses and research laboratories into the town, which forms part of the Northern Metropolis mega project, should also look to collaborate with other universities.

She noted that she expects the institutions to discuss cooperation during the early planning and design stage.

"High-end intelligent manufacturing includes many aspects and is closely related to artificial intelligence and the latest innovation and technology," she said.

"So when institutions bring courses or research laboratories into the Northern Metropolis development, we hope they will be interdisciplinary, cross-industry, or able to cooperate across institutions."

Regarding the Hung Shui Kiu university town development, Choi said she trusts that institutions are in discussions with the industry.

The three Hung Shui Kiu campus area sites, totalling about 26 hectares, are open for applications until December 31.

The project, one of three university towns planned for the Northern Metropolis, is the first to be launched. Choi said each of the three sites has attracted interest from institutions.

The collaboration push comes as the government expects loan applications for the university town to exceed the HK$10 billion originally earmarked because the sites are larger than first planned.

Choi said the HK$10 billion should be enough to start the project and that the government would seek additional funding if needed.

She went on to say that proposals would be assessed comprehensively, taking into account the financial strength and development strategies of the educational organisations.

Edited by Azam Khan

articles.title: 'Decision on Wang Fuk site's future may take years'
articles.excerpt: Acting Housing Secretary Michael Wong on Saturday said the long-term future of the Wang Fuk Court site could take years…
articles.fullText:
Acting Housing Secretary Michael Wong on Saturday said the long-term future of the Wang Fuk Court site could take years to finalise.

Wong, who is also the deputy financial secretary, was speaking on Commercial Radio, two days after the first anniversary of the fire at the Tai Po Estate that killed 168 people.

The government has made it clear that the site will not be used for redevelopment or profit but for community facilities or a park once the land is recovered.

"Consolidating ownership rights and the eventual demolition of the buildings will also require time," he said.

"These relevant procedures will be carried out over the coming years.

"As for the specific nature of the park and the associated community facilities, there will be opportunities to discuss and address these matters with the community in the years ahead."

When asked whether a memorial park would be built, similar to memorials created after the Sichuan earthquake in 2008 and the 9/11 attacks, Wong said he would not speculate on specifics at this stage.

"This is a serious matter that requires consideration for the feelings of various stakeholders," he said.

"The process will span several years and involve aspects such as land planning and the specific design of the park. Therefore, I do not intend to speculate on the details."

Edited by Robert Kemp

articles.title: Race to pave way for smooth run as Route 6 fully opens
articles.excerpt: Transport officials are stepping up signage and driver guidance to help motorists adapt to the new road layout ahead of…
articles.fullText:
Transport officials are stepping up signage and driver guidance to help motorists adapt to the new road layout ahead of Route 6's full opening on December 6.

The Central Kowloon Bypass will open to traffic at 7 am that day. Its completion marks the finishing piece of Route 6.

Leung Sai-ho, Deputy Commissioner for Transport (planning and technical services), said the extra signage is intended to give drivers earlier and clearer warnings before junctions, including advance notices about 100 to 200 metres before a lane-change point.

"All drivers need time to adapt," he said on an RTHK programme, acknowledging that the opening of the Yau Ma Tei section last year had shown some motorists making late or dangerous lane changes.

"For the opening of the Kowloon Bay section, we have over 80 temporary road signs – that is, the yellow ones – which everyone can see are clearly new.

"The yellow signs are specifically for the opening period to help everyone adapt.

"Of course, we also have the original blue, more permanent signs, which everyone can continue to use. These yellow signs are mainly placed at fork junctions where everyone needs to make decisions."

Officials have also changed road markings at key decision points.

At the Cha Kwo Ling roundabout, for example, a dashed-and-solid line arrangement has been implemented so drivers who have taken the fast lane can shift back to the slow lane safely before continuing through the roundabout.

Authorities are also urging drivers not to panic if they pick the wrong lane.

"Hong Kong is a relatively small place, so even if you choose the wrong lane, you can quickly return to your destination," Leung said.

"Please don’t do something that violates traffic signs for a moment’s convenience because it does affect your safety."

The Transport Department has posted driving-guide videos on its website showing the recommended lanes for different destinations.

Officials advise motorists to review their routes before setting off and to budget extra time for their drives on December 7, the first working day after the Sunday opening, when traffic may be heavier as drivers try the new route.

Edited by Robert Kemp

articles.title: US attacks cargo ship 'trying to run Iran blockade'
articles.excerpt: The US military says it disabled a Palau-flagged bulk carrier violating Washington's blockade of Iranian ports. Central Command (Centcom), which…
articles.fullText:
The US military says it disabled a Palau-flagged bulk carrier violating Washington's blockade of Iranian ports.

Central Command (Centcom), which oversees US forces in the Middle East, said on Friday its aircraft had fired "precision munitions" on Thursday into the Pacific Archer's stern after it attempted to run the blockade.

"The ship's propulsion was ultimately disabled and the civilian crew was unharmed," it said, noting the incident occurred in the Gulf of Oman.

The Pacific Archer had left Bandar Abbas, an Iranian port on the Strait of Hormuz, it said.

Centcom said it "continues to strictly enforce the blockade", which has seen six ships disabled and 158 others redirected.

The United States launched its blockade in mid-July following the collapse of a short-lived agreement with Iran.

Iran has meanwhile sought to impose its own blockade on ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz.

Iranian forces have made multiple announcements in recent weeks of ships catching fire attempting to use routes that Tehran considers off-limits.

On Monday, Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei vowed to use all means at the country's disposal to counter the US blockade.

Diplomatic efforts to resolve the crisis – which broke out in late February with US and Israeli attacks on Iran – remain stalled, especially since the collapse of a June deal that laid out a pathway to a permanent settlement.

Iran has said Hormuz could be open within two days but only if Washington agreed to its list of demands, which include the lifting of the blockade. (AFP)

Edited by Robert Kemp

articles.title: Taiwan’s elections offer Hong Kong and Chinese migrants freedoms denied at home
articles.excerpt: From casting their first ballots to joining campaign rallies, new immigrants embrace democracy in Taiwan.
articles.fullText:
On the final Sunday before Taiwan’s Nov. 28 local elections, Hong Kong exile Tong Wai-hung and his wife, To Yee-lan, took to the streets of Taipei, listening to campaign speeches, watching performances and exchanging election souvenirs with Taiwanese voters.
For the couple, who fled Hong Kong after taking part in its pro-democracy movement, what might seem like an ordinary day of campaigning in Taiwan was a reminder of what they had lost back home.
“Isn’t this what elections are supposed to be like?” Tong wrote on social media.
As Taiwanese voters head to the polls to elect local leaders in a vote widely seen as a bellwether for the 2028 presidential election, immigrants from Hong Kong and mainland China are embracing an opportunity to experience competitive democratic elections – a political freedom denied to them in their homelands.
Some are eligible to cast their first ballots as Taiwanese citizens, while others have taken part in campaign rallies, signed up as election monitors and encouraged Taiwanese friends to exercise a right many have come to take for granted.
The day before the Taipei campaign events, Tong watched a livestream of a mayoral candidate’s motorcade in Taichung, where a group of people held up signs identifying themselves as “Hongkongers with voting rights.”
“Hongkongers now speak up more for Taiwan’s democracy and freedom than for Hong Kong’s democracy and freedom, because fighting for democracy and freedom in Hong Kong can get you arrested,” he said.
Hong Kong immigrants in Taiwan hold up signs reading “Hongkongers with voting rights” as they take part in election campaign activities.
(Screenshot from Puma Shen’s YouTube livestream) A vote for the first time
Among those eligible to vote for the first time is Choi Chi-ho, a former Hong Kong protester who arrived in Taiwan bearing scars from beanbag rounds used by police to suppress street demonstrations during the 2019 protests against a proposed extradition bill.
“It has now been seven years and four months since I came to Taiwan in exile. I received my identity card on June 16 last year,” Choi said, recalling the dates precisely.
Six months ago, he completed his military service, becoming the first Hong Kong protester to serve in Taiwan’s armed forces.
A political science student, Choi said he had previously felt somewhat like an outsider without the right to vote. Being able to defend Taiwan’s democracy through the ballot box has given him a greater sense of belonging.
Several campaign ribbons hang from his backpack, including a rainbow-colored one given to him by a Hong Kong friend who visited Taiwan for its LGBTQ pride parade.
“He felt it might be dangerous to take it back,” Choi said. “For Hongkongers living in Hong Kong now, even expressing where they stand involves considerable risk.”
For Choi, relations with Beijing remain an important consideration at the ballot box, even though cross-strait issues have not featured prominently in the local election campaigns.
“As a Hong Kong protester, when we consider whom to vote for, we will absolutely not vote for anyone who is pro-Communist,” he said.
Choi Chi-ho, the first Hong Kong protester to serve in Taiwan’s military, received his certificate of completion after finishing his military service in March 2026.
(Choi Chi-ho) Fan Gong, a native of Wenzhou in China’s eastern Zhejiang province, is also experiencing democratic election campaigning for the first time.
Married to a Taiwanese woman for four years, Fan moved to her hometown in Miaoli two years ago amid concerns about their children’s education and food safety. The couple now runs a small noodle restaurant, decorated inside and out with campaign posters and ribbons from various candidates.
Fan said he supported all political parties opposed to the Chinese Communist Party and had signed up to volunteer as an election observer outside a polling station.
“Taiwan represents the pinnacle of the Chinese-speaking world,” Fan said.
“I’m very excited, because in China there is no such process in which the entire population participates in elections.”
From ‘Be Water’ to a wave of democracy
One distinctive feature of this year’s election has been the proliferation of colorful campaign ribbons, part of a grassroots phenomenon known as “ocean currents.”
The trend began with supporters of Democratic Progressive Party Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen, who independently designed ribbons and campaign souvenirs. The campaign of his Kuomintang rival, Chiang Wan-an, and candidates elsewhere subsequently introduced their own versions.
Tied around wrists, backpacks and motorcycles, the ribbons have become a means of expressing political preferences and connecting with like-minded voters.
For former Hong Kong protesters, the spontaneous mobilization is reminiscent of the “Be Water” philosophy of the 2019 pro-democracy movement.
“The spontaneous mobilization of citizens is very similar,” Tong said. “People come out naturally, and those who share common values gather together and gradually form a force.”
Choi acknowledged that a protest movement and an election were fundamentally different, but said both demonstrated how individual actions could collectively shape society.
Tong’s Muay Thai studio in Taipei has effectively become an informal election gathering point. What began with a single origami boat placed in a locker has grown into a collection of campaign ribbons, stickers and badges brought in by students to exchange.
“There are more and more campaign souvenirs here, just like cells gradually dividing on their own,” he said.
Tong, who expects to obtain his Taiwanese identity card and voting rights next year, has attended campaign events across party lines to learn about the island’s electoral system.
“I wonder, if one day we really can return to Hong Kong, can we bring Taiwan’s system back to Hong Kong? What can we take back?” he said.
“I want to study Taiwan’s democratic system and electoral system properly while I’m here.”
The “ocean currents” campaign ribbon movement has sparked a wave of civic engagement across Taiwan, drawing international attention to the island’s vibrant democracy.
(Chiang Ying-ying/AP) Democracy under pressure
The election comes amid concerns about Chinese interference, including online influence operations and financial assistance for Taiwanese businesspeople and their families to return home to vote.
Taiwan’s government has reported nearly 2,700 social media accounts suspected of involvement in Chinese information operations to social media giant Meta.
Fan said his wife had previously received money to cover travel expenses to Taiwan to vote.
“Whatever amount you say the round-trip airfare costs, they will give you more, including accommodation,” he said, adding that efforts were made beforehand to influence voters to support particular political camps and candidates.
For some Hong Kong exiles, pressure from Beijing has followed them to Taiwan.
Tong and his wife, both arrested during the 2019 Hong Kong protests, have continued advocating for democracy in their former home. Their Muay Thai studio was splashed with red paint in separate incidents late last year and early this year.
“The more they suppress us, the more we have to stand up and speak out,” To said. “What they do will not make us increasingly afraid. Instead, it will further strengthen our voices in opposing them.”
The couple purchased the vandalized door from their landlord and put it on display at a human rights exhibition.
Tong Wai-hung had custom-made “ocean currents” pet collars to exchange campaign souvenirs and share his belief in democracy with others.
(Tong Wai-hung) The power of a ballot
For these immigrants, participating in Taiwan’s democracy also means persuading others not to underestimate the value of their political freedoms.
“Seeing the freedom and democracy Taiwan enjoys today, I’m actually very envious, and I’m also very worried for you,” Fan said. “Once some things are lost, they can never be recovered.”
“I hope that through my own efforts I can influence others to exercise their civic rights and vote for the kind of life they want.”
At Tong’s boxing studio, a young student once told him that he had never voted and had no intention of doing so in this election.
Tong told him about Hong Kong.
When he asked the student again a few days ago whether he planned to vote, the answer had changed: he would.
“I don’t know whom he will vote for, because I believe he has the right to choose freely. He can vote for anyone, but he must cast his ballot,” Tong said with a smile.
“Your votes really are your power. You really do have the power to change this society.”
Edited by Taejun Kang .

articles.title: Chelsea lose again, going down to Nottingham Forest
articles.excerpt: Chelsea suffered an embarrassing 3-2 defeat at Nottingham Forest on Friday as Morgan Gibbs-White's double piled pressure on beleaguered Blues…
articles.fullText:
Chelsea suffered an embarrassing 3-2 defeat at Nottingham Forest on Friday as Morgan Gibbs-White's double piled pressure on beleaguered Blues boss Xabi Alonso.

Alonso's side crashed to a fourth defeat in their last five Premier League matches after another laboured performance at the City Ground.

Igor Jesus's early opener set the tone for Chelsea's dispiriting evening by the banks of the River Trent.

Gibbs-White's second half penalty increased Forest's lead and Emmanuel Emegha's quick reply proved a false dawn for Chelsea.

Gibbs-White struck again and Emegha's second goal came too late for ashen-faced Alonso as the reality of Chelsea's plight sank in.

After last weekend's dismal 4-1 home loss to Leeds, Chelsea's tame surrender was the last thing Alonso needed as he struggles in his first season in charge.

Chelsea are languishing in eighth place after a sixth defeat in their 12 league games under Alonso, a position that is likely to get even worse after the rest of the weekend's fixtures.

Chelsea's third successive defeat will inevitably trigger speculation that Alonso is in danger of being sacked after a miserable start to his first spell as a Premier League manager.

The absence of injured Brazilian striker Joao Pedro has stalled Chelsea's previously powerful attack, while their error-prone defence has already shipped 23 league goals after allowing lowly Forest to run riot.

Failure to beat bottom of the table Crystal Palace on Wednesday would turn the heat up even further on the former Real Madrid and Bayer Leverkusen boss.

Admitting his team needed "strong characters and big personalities", Alonso handed starts to vastly experienced duo Jordan Henderson and Danny Welbeck.

But Chelsea's grizzled veterans could do nothing to stop Forest taking the lead in eye-catching style in the fifth minute.

Daniel Munoz's cross arrowed towards Jesus 12 yards from goal and the Brazilian unleashed a blistering volley that flashed into the top corner as Chelsea keeper Emiliano Martinez grasped at thin air.

Chelsea struggled to respond to that blow and even when they had a rare sight of goal, Morgan Rogers blazed wildly over.

Despite having Levi Colwill available, Alonso opted to start Ecuador midfielder Moises Caicedo at centre-back in a move that backfired badly.

Intriguingly, Wesley Fofana featured for Chelsea after apologising for a controversial YouTube interview in which the defender joked about his penalty miss in a League Cup shoot-out defeat against Liverpool this season.

The Chelsea fans packed into one end of the City Ground weren't as forgiving as Alonso, subjecting Fofana to jeers whenever he touched the ball.

The Blues were desperately short of intensity and rhythm, mustering just three touches in the Forest area in the first half, so Alonso sent on Emegha for Welbeck at the interval.

But the striker's introduction ignored the holes in Chelsea's porous defence and their situation grew more desperate in the 51st minute.

Fofana's approval rating with Chelsea supporters plunged even lower as he carelessly bundled over former Blues striker Liam Delap to concede a penalty that Gibbs-White dispatched with ease.

Fofana was hauled off to save him from any further opprobrium.

Emegha reduced the deficit three minutes later, firing into the bottom corner after Pedro Neto's effort deflected to him 10 yards from goal.

Alonso's men tried to rally, appealing in vain for a penalty after Jair Cunha's arm made contact with the ball.

But Forest delivered the knockout blow in the 72nd minute.

Xaver Schlager floated a pin-point pass behind the flat-footed Chelsea defence and Gibbs-White made a perfectly-timed run to clip a composed shot past Martinez from close-range.

Emegha's 89th minute strike gave the scoreline a more flattering look than Chelsea deserved for a moribund performance. (AFP)

Edited by Robert Kemp

articles.title: Wall Street ends shortened trading day on a high note
articles.excerpt: US stock markets ended higher on Friday, closing out a shortened trading week marked by both a surge in stock…
articles.fullText:
US stock markets ended higher on Friday, closing out a shortened trading week marked by both a surge in stock indexes and heavy selling of technology shares.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 1.2 percent to 50,775, the Nasdaq Composite rose 2.3 percent to 24,129, and the S&P 500 rose 1.6 percent to 7,297.

After shutting for Thanksgiving on Thursday, US markets closed early on Friday.

As Black Friday shopping got underway, online retail giant Amazon gained 4 percent.

The biggest gains came from stocks directly linked to artificial intelligence, including chipmakers Micron and AMD. Memory specialist SanDisk surged nearly 16 percent.

Only tech giant Nvidia posted more modest gains, edging up just 0.80 percent. (AFP)

Edited by Robert Kemp

articles.title: Hamas accuses Israel of attack on son of Hamas chief
articles.excerpt: Hamas said Israel tried to kill an adult son of the Palestinian movement's chief Khalil al-Hayya in an overnight strike…
articles.fullText:
Hamas said Israel tried to kill an adult son of the Palestinian movement's chief Khalil al-Hayya in an overnight strike on Friday, with a Gaza security source telling AFP he survived.

The strike follows a series of killings by the Israeli military in recent days that have targeted Hamas officials, despite a ceasefire in the war-shattered Palestinian territory.

Separately, Gaza's civil defence agency said Israeli forces killed seven people across the territory on Friday.

"Izz al-Din al-Hayya, the youngest surviving son of Hamas political bureau chief Khalil al-Hayya, along with his family and the family of his late brother Azzam, survived an Israeli assassination attempt early on Friday targeting a residential apartment in the Rimal neighbourhood, west of Gaza City," a security source in Gaza told AFP.

When asked by AFP, the Israeli military said it was looking into the incident.

Bassem Naim, a member of the Palestinian Islamist movement's political bureau, said "Israel's attempt to target the youngest son of Hamas political bureau chief Khalil al-Hayya... constitutes 'state terrorism,'" while Hamas issued a statement calling the targeting "cowardly".

Four of al-Hayya's sons have already been killed in Israeli attacks, including one in May and another in an Israeli strike targeting Hamas leaders in Doha in September 2025.

Two others were killed before the Gaza war, which was triggered by Hamas's October 7, 2023 attack on Israel.

Gaza's civil defence agency, a rescue force which operates under Hamas authority, said an Israeli drone strike west of Rafah city in southern Gaza killed three people on Friday, with nearby Nasser Hospital confirming it received three bodies following the strike.

The Israeli military said it had struck "three terrorists in the area".

Another drone strike west of Jabalia refugee camp in northern Gaza killed one person, the civil defence and Al-Shifa Hospital said.

The Israeli military said it was checking the incident.

The civil defence agency said two more people were killed in an Israeli drone strike near Gaza City's Al-Shifa Hospital, with the medical facility confirming it received two bodies.

The Israeli military told AFP it struck "a terrorist in the area," adding that there was "no harm to the hospital or any medical practice" in the vicinity.

Israeli gunfire in the Rafah area killed another person, the civil defence said. The Israeli military said it was checking that incident.

Israel and Hamas regularly accuse each other of violating the ceasefire that came into effect in October 2025, after two years of devastating war.

More than 1,650 Palestinians have been killed since the start of the truce, according to an AFP tally based on data from the Gaza health ministry, which also operates under Hamas authority and whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations.

In the same period, the Israeli military says seven of its soldiers have been killed, as well as one civilian contractor. (AFP)

Edited by Robert Kemp

articles.title: AI bionic eye breakthrough could help restore sight
articles.excerpt: An AI bionic eye trained on a blind man's brain responses helped UC Santa Barbara researchers produce more predictable phosphenes…
articles.fullText:
At a hospital in Spain, a 27-year-old man who lost his sight after a traumatic brain injury reported seeing flashes of light when researchers stimulated part of his brain. Those flashes were limited, but scientists have now used artificial intelligence to gain more control over the brain activity behind them.
The research could help make future artificial vision systems more reliable. Scientists are developing an AI bionic eye approach that learns how an individual's brain responds to electrical stimulation. Although the technology remains experimental , it could eventually help people who have lost their sight regain some degree of vision. 
So, how does this brain implant work, and what would it take to turn a few flashes of light into useful vision?
MOUTHPAD LETS YOUR TONGUE CONTROL A COMPUTER
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.
Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
When you look at something, your eyes send signals to your brain, which processes what you're seeing. But what happens when those signals can no longer reach the brain? For years, scientists have been developing electronic implants that attempt to restore some vision. 
Some stimulate the retina, the light-sensitive tissue at the back of the eye. Others take a different approach by sending electrical signals directly to the brain. That's what makes this research interesting. Scientists are studying a device called a visual cortical prosthesis, sometimes described as a bionic eye. Despite the nickname, the implant goes into the brain rather than the eye.
It targets the visual cortex, the part of the brain responsible for processing visual information. When researchers stimulate this area with electricity, a person may experience flashes or spots of light known as phosphenes. These sensations can resemble glowing dots or simple shapes. However, getting the brain to produce consistent results has been a major challenge.
In 2024, researchers from UC Santa Barbara traveled to Spain as part of a collaborative study with ETH Zurich and Miguel Hernández University involving a 27-year-old man who had lost his sight after a traumatic brain injury. At IMED Elche Hospital, the man had received an experimental implant containing 96 electrodes placed in his visual cortex. The device was intended to remain implanted for six months before being removed.
During the study, researchers delivered small electrical currents through the electrodes. The man reported experiencing flashes of light and various shapes. That was encouraging, but the researchers wanted to go further. They needed to understand why certain electrical signals produced particular sensations and whether those responses could become more predictable.
FIRST-EVER GENE THERAPY FOR HEARING LOSS GETS FDA APPROVAL: 'GROUNDBREAKING'
This is where artificial intelligence helped the researchers make progress. Scientists trained a deep learning model to study how the man's brain responded to different electrical stimulation patterns. Instead of relying solely on the settings sent to the electrodes, the AI analyzed the actual brain activity those signals produced. It also considered what the brain was doing immediately before stimulation. 
That's important because brain activity can fluctuate over time, which can affect how someone responds to the same electrical signals.
Using this information, researchers identified stimulation patterns more likely to produce particular brain responses . When they tested those AI-designed patterns, the results improved. The researchers achieved greater accuracy in producing their intended patterns of brain activity while using less electrical current. They also discovered something important. 
The brain activity recorded after stimulation was a better predictor of what the man reported seeing than the electrical settings alone. In other words, knowing how the brain responded gave researchers a better indication of the man's visual experience.
Michael Beyeler, an associate professor at UC Santa Barbara who helped lead the research, explained the goal.
"Ultimately, the device should adapt to the person, not the other way around," he said.
That approach could help future implants adjust to changes in brain activity rather than depend on the same stimulation settings every time. The research was published in the journal Neuron.
It's an exciting possibility, but there's still a long road ahead. The man in this experiment experienced flashes and shapes of light. He did not regain normal eyesight, and researchers have yet to demonstrate that this AI approach can provide the functional vision someone would need to read or recognize faces. The experiment also involved only one participant. Scientists need additional research to determine how well the approach works in other people.
Still, the findings address a significant challenge. Researchers can stimulate the brain, but predicting exactly what someone will experience has been difficult. AI could help close that gap by learning how each person's brain responds and identifying better ways to deliver electrical signals. We've also covered a tiny retinal implant that helped people with advanced age-related macular degeneration regain some central vision. 
That device works with the retina and specialized glasses. The new research takes a different route by targeting the brain directly. It could eventually offer another option for people whose eyes or optic nerves can no longer send visual information effectively, provided their visual cortex can still respond to stimulation.
ROBOT PERFORMS 26 CATARACT SURGERIES WITH SURGEON CONTROL
Researchers still have several challenges to overcome before this technology could become a practical treatment . First, they need to demonstrate that the approach works safely and consistently in more people. Scientists must also determine whether the flashes and shapes produced by electrical stimulation can become useful visual information. Another challenge involves keeping the implant responsive as the brain changes. 
A stimulation pattern that works during one session may produce different results later.
The AI approach tested in this study offers a possible way to address that problem. However, researchers have yet to demonstrate a complete system that continuously adapts and delivers useful vision during everyday activities. For people dealing with vision loss today, technology already provides other forms of assistance. 
Our article on tech tools that make vision loss easier to manage at CyberGuy.com explores features that can help with everyday tasks. As for this new research, the next challenge involves turning more predictable brain responses into visual experiences that could help someone navigate the world.
The possibility of helping someone regain their sight through a brain implant is pretty remarkable. What I find especially interesting about this research is how AI could help scientists understand the way each person's brain responds to electrical signals. That could eventually make artificial vision more reliable. But there's still a big difference between seeing flashes of light and being able to recognize what's around you. I'd love to see this technology reach a point where someone who has lost their sight can recognize familiar objects or move around more independently. We're not there yet, and this was only one participant. Still, if researchers can turn these early results into useful vision, it could make an enormous difference in people's lives.
If scientists could someday restore even a small amount of your vision through a brain implant, would you consider the surgery, or would you wait until the technology could provide clearer sight? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com

articles.title: FS visits Dutch health tech firm
articles.excerpt: Financial Secretary Paul Chan visited the research and development (R&D) campus of a major Dutch health technology firm and attended…
articles.fullText:
Financial Secretary Paul Chan visited the research and development (R&D) campus of a major Dutch health technology firm and attended a luncheon hosted by a major Dutch bank during his trip to the Netherlands.

Continuing his visit yesterday, Mr Chan led a Hong Kong business and innovation and technology (I&T) delegation to the Dutch city of Eindhoven.

Visiting the R&D campus of Philips in Best, a major Dutch health technology company, he got a firsthand look at its latest breakthroughs in diagnostic imaging, image-guided therapy and artificial intelligence (AI) applications in healthcare.

In a follow-up exchange, the financial chief underscored Hong Kong's push to become an international I&T centre - highlighting the new measures to boost artificial intelligence and medical research outlined in Hong Kong’s first Five-Year Plan.

He also called on the company to expand its research and innovation footprint in Hong Kong to help bring more health-tech breakthroughs to market.

Later in the day, Mr Chan and the delegation attended a luncheon hosted by a major Dutch bank, where they were briefed on Europe’s latest economic outlook and explored new avenues for bilateral co-operation.

As part of his itinerary, Mr Chan also met with the management of a major global alternative investment and asset management administration firm, where he was briefed on its business in Europe, Asia and Hong Kong.

In turn, Mr Chan introduced them to the latest developments in Hong Kong's asset and wealth management industry, as well as the policy measures designed to attract various types of funds, family offices and high-net-worth individuals to Hong Kong.

He encouraged the firm to leverage the Hong Kong platform to help its clients expand their business in Asia.

The Financial Secretary and the delegation will conclude their visit to the Netherlands today, and he will arrive back in Hong Kong tomorrow morning.

articles.title: Fake driving licence agents flagged
articles.excerpt: The Transport Department today urged the public not to fall for bogus messages on social media touting assistance in applying…
articles.fullText:
The Transport Department today urged the public not to fall for bogus messages on social media touting assistance in applying for the direct issue of a Hong Kong full driving licence without supporting documents, and to stay vigilant against deception.

The department pointed out that it has no connection with these "agents", adding that any Hong Kong driving licence obtained using false documents will be cancelled, and the case will be referred to law enforcement agencies for follow-up.

The department emphasised that it always rigorously verifies every application for direct issue and exercises strict gatekeeping. Applicants must fully comply with the relevant statutory requirements and provide true and accurate supporting documents, regardless of whether they submit applications in person or through an authorised agent.

When in doubt, the department will contact the relevant consulate or transport authority for verification. It also has an established mechanism with Mainland vehicle administration offices to verify questionable Mainland driving licences. Any cases contravening legal requirements will be referred to law enforcement agencies for follow-up.

For a Hong Kong resident applying for direct issue, even if they hold a valid Mainland full driving licence and have passed the relevant driving test, they must satisfy specific requirements.

Specifically, the Mainland driving licence must have been issued during a period of residence in the Mainland of not less than six months; alternatively, the applicant must have held the Mainland driving licence for not less than five years, or hold a Mainland passport or other equivalent travel document.

Applicants must provide the originals of various supporting documents for on-site verification, including a valid domestic driving licence, a passport or other travel document, and proof of residence.

Under the Road Traffic Ordinance, any person who makes a false statement for the purpose of obtaining a driving licence commits an offence and is liable on conviction to a maximum fine of $5,000 and six months' imprisonment.

articles.title: Hackers breach US Air Force cloud computing platform
articles.excerpt: Hackers have breached the US Air Force's flagship cloud computing platform, three people familiar with the matter told Reuters, in…
articles.fullText:
Hackers have breached the US Air Force's flagship cloud computing platform, three people familiar with the matter told Reuters, in a development that could jeopardise a vast swathe of sensitive tactical, personnel and logistics data.

The intrusion at Cloud One was discovered within the past month or so during work to upgrade the system, two of the people said, adding that the discovery has led to disruption across the platform.

Reuters could not establish the identity of the hackers, the full scope of the intrusion or whether any data had been stolen.

In a statement to Reuters, the Air Force said it "does not comment on the security posture, vulnerabilities or operational status of specific networks and systems".

"We continuously take prudent measures to protect Department (of the Air Force) information, systems and mission capabilities," it added.

Initiated in 2017, Cloud One was meant to serve as a one-stop shop for the Air Force's IT needs, combining the resources of four operators — Microsoft, Amazon, Oracle and Alphabet — to power scores of applications including those that manage personnel data and pay or logistics and maintenance.

Among them are the Air Force's Cloud-Based Command and Control, which collates air defence radar and other data feeds from across North America, and the Theater Integrated Combat Munitions System, which tracks bombs and missiles across more than 200 US Air Force locations worldwide.

Cloud One is among the US military's largest cloud platforms, according to two sources.

"A breach here is a big deal," one source said.

Investigators have called in Cyber Command, the US military's cyber force, to assess the damage, one source said. Cyber Command did not respond to requests for comment.

The news of the breach comes amid heightened anxiety over AI-powered intrusions, a particularly serious problem for cloud-based networks because AI models can swiftly detect weaknesses across wide surface areas.

The US government has already been dealing with the fallout from at least six other recently disclosed cyber incidents, including two at the FBI, a previous hack of Pentagon data, a recent leak of Department of Homeland Security personnel information, a breach affecting at least two spy agencies and a hack at the Treasury Department. (Reuters)

Edited by Raymond Yeung

articles.title: Personal data of 7,500 Octopus users leaked
articles.excerpt: Some 7,500 Octopus users have had their personal data leaked following a cyberattack, the company has said, though it stressed…
articles.fullText:
Some 7,500 Octopus users have had their personal data leaked following a cyberattack, the company has said, though it stressed that it has not detected any financial loss by customers.

In a statement, the operator of the electronic payment system said it detected abnormal activity from a cyberattack on Friday morning.

The compromised customer data included personal information such as names and photographs.

Octopus said some users of its "Automatic Add Value Service" also had their bank codes and top-up amounts accessed, but stressed that no credit card or bank account information was leaked.

In addition, data belonging to about 22,000 merchants was compromised in the incident, involving the names, titles, email addresses, and the phone numbers of merchants' contact persons.

The company said core Octopus services continue to operate normally, with only a small number of features temporarily affected as a precautionary measure.

A thorough investigation is under way, Octopus said, adding that affected customers will be contacted directly.

Members of the public are urged to watch for unusual account activity and stay alert for suspicious calls, SMS messages, emails, or links.

Edited by Raymond Yeung

articles.title: Google Gemini may expose private emails to reviewers
articles.excerpt: A researcher claims Google Gemini pulled private Gmail billing details into chats, and Google confirms some connected-app data may face…
articles.fullText:
Think about everything sitting in your Gmail inbox right now. Maybe there's a conversation with your doctor, a recent bank statement or a personal message you never intended anyone else to read. Your Google Drive may hold years of private documents. You probably don't spend much time thinking about who might see that information beyond the people you share it with. But what happens when you connect those services to Google's Gemini AI assistant ?
An independent researcher has raised concerns about how Gemini handles information retrieved from connected Gmail and Google Drive accounts. The findings prompted questions about whether some private content could end up in conversations reviewed by humans.
We contacted Google, and the company confirmed that some information retrieved from connected Gmail and Drive accounts may be seen by human reviewers under certain circumstances. Google stressed that these connections are off by default. Here's what you should know before giving Gemini access to your personal information.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.
Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
AI CHATBOT PRIVACY: WHAT YOUR AI MAY KNOW ABOUT YOU
An independent researcher using the name thisisme6598 published findings on GitHub, raising questions about the way Gemini retrieves information from connected Gmail and Google Drive accounts . The researcher tested Gemini using a personal Google Account with connected apps enabled. According to the published findings, Gemini sometimes retrieved information from emails or files during conversations without someone explicitly asking it to search Gmail or Drive. For example, the researcher described asking Gemini whether an internet service bill seemed too expensive. During some tests, Gemini reportedly retrieved billing information from Gmail, including payment amounts, account details and confirmation numbers.
In certain instances, the researcher reported that Gemini returned several sentences directly from an email and, in some tests, the entire email, including its headers. The researcher argues that this behavior creates a privacy concern because information retrieved into a Gemini conversation may become eligible for human review. However, the published findings do not establish that a human reviewer actually accessed the researcher's emails. Google told CyberGuy that the reported retrieval was standard behavior for someone who had voluntarily connected their apps. The company also emphasized that retrieved files remain visible only to the authenticated account holder and are not exposed publicly through this process.
Yes, under certain circumstances. Google's own Connected Apps privacy documentation confirms that trained human reviewers, including service providers, may review a subset of information processed through Gemini's connected apps. That information can include summaries or excerpts from relevant Gmail messages and Google Drive documents.
In some cases, Google acknowledges that reviewers may see a complete email or file if it is short or especially relevant to the request. Google also says human reviewers may access some Gmail inbox content when investigating abuse or harm or responding to submitted feedback.
The company uses these reviews to evaluate Gemini's responses and improve its services.
Simply using Gmail or Google Drive does not subject your private content to this review process. The concern involves information retrieved after someone voluntarily connects those services to consumer Gemini. Google says it does not train generative AI models directly on someone's entire Gmail inbox or Drive. However, relevant information processed during Gemini conversations may be used for model improvement, depending on account settings. Google specifically warns against connecting apps containing confidential information someone would be uncomfortable having a reviewer see.
We contacted Google directly to ask whether human reviewers could access Gmail messages or Drive files processed through the consumer Gemini app. We also asked whether the company had changed its privacy disclosures, notified existing customers and provided ways to prevent human review. A Google spokesperson told CyberGuy:
"Gmail and Google Drive’s core privacy protections remain unchanged, and your private emails and files are not reviewed by humans simply by using Gmail, Drive, or built-in Workspace features. Connecting those apps to the consumer Gemini app is off by default — it’s an optional way to get more personalized, time-saving answers across your Google apps when you want them. Users can disconnect their apps in Gemini settings at any time without losing access to Gemini’s core features."
Google also confirmed that when someone connects their apps to consumer Gemini with activity saving enabled, a small subset of conversations may undergo human review. Those conversations can contain relevant information retrieved from connected services. Before trained service providers review the material, Google says it separates the conversations from the associated Google Account and takes steps to reduce identifying information. The company also disputes the suggestion that the researcher's findings demonstrate public exposure of private files.
Another part of the controversy involves changes to Google's public privacy disclosures . In Oct. 2023, Google published a blog post about its approach to generative AI privacy. The company said that content from Gmail, Docs and Drive accessed through Bard's Workspace extensions would not be seen by human reviewers or used to train the Bard model.
On Oct. 16, 2026, Google added an update to that same blog post. The new language explains that Google has introduced additional optional features allowing people to connect Workspace information to other Google services. Google says that when someone enables these newer features, a subset of the information may be used to train generative AI models, depending on their settings. It may also undergo human review in limited circumstances. The researcher argues that the change represents a reversal of Google's earlier privacy commitment.
However, Google's original statement concerned Bard's Workspace extensions, while the updated disclosure addresses newer connected features. The available evidence does not establish that Google quietly changed the underlying handling of information in existing connections. We asked Google whether people who previously connected their accounts were notified about the updated disclosures or asked to provide additional consent. Google's response did not directly address those questions. Instead, the company emphasized that the newer connections are optional and can be disabled. That leaves an important question about how clearly Google communicates changes to its AI privacy practices, particularly as new features gain access to more personal information.
APPLE TIGHTENS MAC SECURITY AS AI AGENTS SEEK YOUR FILES
Google says it disconnects conversations from the associated Google Account before sending them to trained service providers for routine review. The company also takes steps to reduce personal information. However, removing account identifiers does not necessarily eliminate every sensitive detail contained in an email excerpt or document summary.
Google's Gemini Apps Privacy Hub explains that conversations reviewed by service providers may be retained for up to three years, even after someone deletes the corresponding activity from their Google Account.
Turning off Gemini's History setting , previously called Keep Activity, prevents future conversations from being used to train generative AI models unless someone submits feedback. However, Google may still process conversations for security and safety purposes, including with help from human reviewers.
On Nov. 16, 2026, Google announced changes to its Gemini privacy controls. Under the previous policy, Google retained conversations for up to 72 hours when Keep Activity was turned off. Under the new policy, Google will retain conversations for approximately two months when History is turned off. The company is rolling out these changes globally over several weeks.
If you use Gemini, it's worth checking which accounts and services you've connected. You may find that you don't need every feature enabled. Here are some settings worth reviewing.
Google groups Gmail and Drive under Google Workspace in its connected-app settings. Here's how to check the connection on a computer.
If you see a different menu, look for Connected Apps in Gemini's settings. Google offers different connection controls depending on account eligibility and available features. You can reconnect supported services later if you decide to use them.
If you want to prevent future conversations from being used to train Google's generative AI models, review this setting.
Turning off History stops future chats from being used to train generative AI models unless you choose to submit feedback. Some connected apps, including Google Workspace, become unavailable. Google may still process conversations for security and safety purposes. Depending on whether the latest privacy update has reached your account, conversations may be retained for up to 72 hours under the previous policy or approximately two months under the new policy.
WHAT YOUR INTERNET PROVIDER, WEBSITES AND ADVERTISERS SEE
Google is introducing a separate privacy control that lets you keep your Gemini conversation history while opting out of generative AI model training. If the new setting is available on your account, here's how to find it on a computer.
Google says future chats will no longer be used to train generative AI models unless you submit feedback. However, human review may still occur for other service improvements and safety purposes. If you want to prevent Gemini from retrieving information from Gmail and Drive, disconnect Google Workspace separately.
Disconnecting an app does not automatically delete information from earlier Gemini conversations. Google says Gemini may still use information from previously saved chats even after you disconnect the original app. That's why it's important to both disconnect the app and delete conversations containing sensitive information.
Remember that previously reviewed information may remain subject to Google's separate retention policies, even after you delete your activity.
Think carefully before giving an AI assistant access to confidential documents or personal communications. If you don't need Gemini to retrieve information from Gmail or Drive , leave those connections disabled. Also, remember that uploading a document directly into Gemini creates a separate privacy consideration.
Google says uploaded content may be used to improve its services when History, previously called Keep Activity, is enabled, potentially with help from human reviewers. Whether that content is used to train generative AI models also depends on your training settings and whether you submit feedback.
Google says the connected-app disclosures involved in this controversy apply to personal Google Accounts using consumer Gemini. Business, Enterprise and Education accounts covered by Google Workspace commercial terms have different privacy protections. According to Google's response to CyberGuy, customer data governed by those commercial terms is not reviewed by humans or used to train foundational AI models.
If you use Gemini through an employer or school, your organization's settings and agreements determine which features are available and how information is handled. The important point is that the consumer Gemini privacy rules discussed here should not automatically be applied to commercial Workspace accounts.
I can understand why someone would want Gemini to search their Gmail or find a document buried in Google Drive. We've all wasted time digging through old emails looking for something we need. Having an AI assistant do that work sounds pretty appealing. But I think Google has a responsibility to make the privacy implications much clearer before someone connects an account. Most people probably don't expect information pulled from their private emails to become part of a conversation that could eventually be reviewed by another human being. I appreciate that Google responded to our questions and explained the safeguards it uses. Still, I would have liked a more direct answer about whether existing customers were notified when the privacy disclosures changed. If you're giving an AI assistant access to years of personal information, you deserve to know exactly how that information might be handled. Personally, I'd leave Gmail and Drive disconnected unless I had a specific reason to use those features.
Would you trust an AI assistant with access to years of your private emails if you knew some of that information could be seen by human reviewers? Or has Google crossed a privacy line, even with your permission? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com.

articles.title: Sanchez in last push to beat right before Spain vote
articles.excerpt: Spain's Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez made a final push to overcome the odds on Friday, the last day of…
articles.fullText:
Spain's Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez made a final push to overcome the odds on Friday, the last day of campaigning for an election this weekend expected to deliver a victory for conservatives and the far right.

The outcome of Sunday's vote will be closely watched as Europe opens an electoral cycle over the next 12 months that could reshape the balance of power within the European Union.

Sanchez has enhanced his global profile in recent years as one of the world's most prominent leftist leaders, but a polarising status at home puts his eight-year tenure in peril.

Polls have consistently put him behind the main right-wing Popular Party (PP), which is predicted to win the most seats in another hung parliament.

It could therefore rely on far-right, anti-immigration Vox, Spain's third-largest political force, which could double its seats and already governs several regions with the PP.

Such a coalition would be a first since Spain's transition to democracy after General Francisco Franco's dictatorship (1939-1975).

Sanchez will hold a final rally in Madrid, seeking a late mobilisation of left-wing voters to defeat what he calls the "regression" of a possible PP-Vox coalition.

PP leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo's campaign finale will be in Seville, capital of the southern Andalusia region, while Vox leader Santiago Abascal will hold a last rally in the eastern city of Valencia.

Some recent polls have suggested the gap between the Socialists and the PP was closing, raising the prospect of another spectacular comeback by Sanchez, seen as the great survivor of Spanish politics.

Sanchez has vaunted his record on the international stage, notably his outspoken defence of immigration, clashes with US President Donald Trump and virulent criticism of Israel.

He has also tried to leverage anger over a housing crisis, passing measures for tenants earlier this month. (AFP)

Edited by Azam Khan

articles.title: 90,000 users compromised in SmartPLAY data breach
articles.excerpt: Around 90,000 users of the government's SmartPLAY booking system for public sports and recreational facilities were involved in a data…
articles.fullText:
Around 90,000 users of the government's SmartPLAY booking system for public sports and recreational facilities were involved in a data breach, according to the Office of the Privacy Commissioner for Personal Data (PCPD).

The privacy watchdog said on Friday that it has launched an investigation after being notified of the incident by the Leisure and Cultural Services Department (LCSD).

The PCPD said that the compromised personal data may include names, gender, dates of birth, addresses, email addresses, and phone numbers.

It reminded members of the public to stay vigilant when they receive unknown or suspicious calls, messages, or emails, and refrain from opening attachments, accessing hyperlinks, or disclosing personal data.

"Even if the caller or message sender is able to state the individual's personal details, they should stop and think before providing further personal data or making payment," the office added.

In a statement, the LCSD said it was informed by the contractor of the breach on Thursday, and immediate measures have since been taken to stop the attack.

"The incident does not involve information on users' identity documents, and SmartPLAY does not store any information on credit cards or other forms of making payments," the statement added.

System managers have also temporarily disabled users from recovering lost passwords, asking them instead to visit a physical venue while checks are being performed.

A separate announcement will be made when the function resumes, the LCSD said.
