articles.title: China investigates Shanghai party chief, raising questions over Xi’s succession plans
articles.excerpt: Chen Jining is the fourth member of the Communist Party’s current Politburo to come under investigation.
articles.fullText:
Read a version of this story in Mandarin .
China has launched an investigation into Shanghai Communist Party chief Chen Jining, and experts told Radio Free Asia that the timing indicates competition has intensified ahead of an anticipated leadership reshuffle at next year’s party congress.
Chen, a member of the ruling Communist Party’s Politburo, is suspected of “serious violations of discipline and law,” authorities announced late on Nov. 24. He is the fourth member of the 20th Politburo to come under investigation, following He Weidong, Zhang Youxia and Ma Xingrui.
Authorities have yet to disclose details of the allegations, announce Chen’s removal from office or name a successor.
Chen’s downfall ahead of the 21st National Congress of the Chinese Communist Party, or CCP, has renewed scrutiny of how Xi intends to shape the next generation of Chinese leaders and whether he will identify a potential successor. Chen was once seen as a potential candidate for the country’s top leadership body.
He had been regarded as a low-profile technocrat with close ties to Xi, Akio Yaita, executive director of the Taipei-based Indo-Pacific Strategy Think Tank, told RFA Mandarin.
Shanghai has historically had a contentious relationship with the central leadership while serving as an important launching pad for local officials seeking positions in Beijing, Yaita said.
A key question, he added, was whether the investigation would remain confined to Chen or extend to other Shanghai officials who had worked with him.
Tightening control over local officials
Hours after the investigation was announced, Shanghai’s Communist Party Standing Committee convened an expanded meeting, expressing its “firm support for the decision of the Party Central Committee” and calling for political discipline to be prioritized and central government directives to be implemented.
Chen, 62, is the first serving Shanghai party chief to come under investigation since Chen Liangyu in 2006. As a result of that investigation, Chen Liangyu was found to have misused funds, was expelled from the CCP, and spent 18 years in prison.
A former president of Tsinghua University, environmental protection minister and Beijing mayor, Chen Jining joined the Politburo in 2022 and succeeded Li Qiang, currently China’s premier, as Shanghai’s party secretary that year.
The post has long been regarded as a stepping stone to China’s highest leadership positions. Xi and Li both previously held the position, as did former President Jiang Zemin and former Premier Zhu Rongji.
Chen Jining, Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party Shanghai Municipal Committee, speaks during the Lujiazui Forum 2025 in Shanghai, China June 18, 2025.
(Brenda Goh/Reuters) Tzeng Wei-feng, an associate research fellow at National Chengchi University’s Institute of International Relations in Taiwan, told RFA Mandarin that the Shanghai leadership’s swift declaration of support for the investigation suggested local officials would increasingly align themselves with Beijing’s policies.
He said the investigations into four Politburo members should be viewed in the context of the party’s Fifth Plenum late last month, which called for strengthened oversight and continued pressure in its anti-corruption campaign.
The expanding powers of party disciplinary authorities, he added, have given Beijing greater leverage over local governments and senior officials.
Yaita suggested that Chen’s extensive exposure to the West may also have worked against him.
Chen spent a decade in Britain and was among the Chinese leadership figures most familiar with Western values, languages and cultures, with the ability to communicate fluently in English with foreign leaders, he said.
At a time when, in Yaita’s view, Xi is increasingly turning China inward and seeking to distance it from the West, a senior official perceived as being overly close to Western countries could arouse Xi’s suspicions.
Succession questions resurface
Chen’s investigation has also renewed attention to the politically sensitive question of Xi’s eventual succession.
Veteran journalist Fang Fei told RFA Mandarin on the sidelines of a press conference in Taiwan that there had been few public indications that Chen was under scrutiny.
She said the successive investigations into senior officials could reflect internal power struggles within the CCP.
While a clear succession plan would help the party ensure a stable transfer of power, Fang said, identifying a successor could also undermine Xi’s authority by creating an alternative center of power.
She cautioned, however, that the opacity of the party’s decision-making made it difficult to determine who else might be implicated in Chen’s case or whether factional rivalries were involved.
Tzeng said Xi’s personal trust in individual officials could carry more weight than their professional expertise or performance in local government when senior leadership appointments are made at the next party congress.
Chinese Politburo Standing Committee member Cai Qi and Chinese President Xi Jinping look on during a bilateral meeting with Vietnam's President To Lam on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen, China Nov. 17, 2026.
(Maxim Shemetov/Reuters) “From this perspective, we can assess that those who remain in office are likely to be members of Xi’s inner circle, such as Cai Qi, as well as those holding lower-risk positions, such as Wang Huning,” he said.
Cai, the former mayor of Beijing, is currently director of the CCP’s General Office, while Wang is the chairman of the National Committee of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference.
U.S.-based economist Cheng Xiaonong, speaking in a previous interview with RFA Mandarin, said the concentration of power in a single leader, rather than the CCP’s previous model of collective leadership, had complicated succession arrangements.
The more concentrated power becomes, Cheng said, the more a leader may fear political retribution after leaving office, while appointing a successor risks allowing that person to establish an independent power base before the transfer of power.
That, he said, was a fundamental dilemma of the CCP’s authoritarian system.
Edited by Taejun Kang and Eugene Whong.

articles.title: Tech billionaire plans 1,000-year floating city at sea
articles.excerpt: Palmer Luckey says SLAB, his floating industrial city, would last 1,000 years, hosting metal processing and oil refining beyond California…
articles.fullText:
How frustrated would you have to be with government red tape to decide the ocean looks like a better place to build a factory? Tech billionaire Palmer Luckey has an answer. He wants to create a massive floating industrial city where American companies could operate beyond certain state and local restrictions.
The project is called SLAB, and Luckey says it would have a design life of 1,000 years. That's a pretty extraordinary promise for something sitting in the middle of the ocean. However, the reasoning behind the project may be even more surprising than the structure itself. We discussed Luckey's ambitious plans in detail on "The CyberGuy Report Podcast" at cyberguy.com/podcast. So, what exactly is he planning to build, and could moving American industry offshore really solve the problems he's trying to escape?
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.
Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
CEO SAYS DOING BUSINESS IN STATE ‘SUCKS’ AS COMPANY HEADS TO TEXAS AMID CALIFORNIA EXODUS
Palmer Luckey, the founder of Oculus and co-founder of defense technology company Anduril Industries, has revealed plans for a floating industrial platform called SLAB . In a November 18 post on X, Luckey explained that he began developing the project after Facebook acquired Oculus in 2014. He used some of the money from that sale to pursue an idea that has fascinated technology entrepreneurs for years.
The concept is known as seasteading. It involves building permanent structures on the ocean where people can live or operate businesses outside some of the restrictions that apply on land. Luckey's version focuses heavily on American industry. He wants to create a place where companies could conduct activities that face significant regulatory hurdles on the mainland. The illustration accompanying his announcement shows an enormous platform rising above the ocean with buildings and industrial facilities on top.
AMERICA'S REDDEST STATE CHASES BILLION-DOLLAR BOOM AS OTHERS SOUR ON MASSIVE EMERGING INDUSTRY
Luckey believes government regulations have made it unnecessarily difficult for certain industries to operate in the United States. His proposed solution is to move some of those operations offshore. He specifically mentioned metal processing and oil refining . He also identified desalination and medical research as possible activities for SLAB. In his announcement, Luckey described the project as a way to strengthen American industry by creating a "relief valve for ill-considered or outdated rules and regulations."
His argument is that companies could operate more efficiently if they avoided certain state and local restrictions. He also wants the offshore platform to be cheaper than building comparable facilities on land, although he has not publicly demonstrated that the economics would work. There is also a more controversial possibility. In a separate exchange on X, Luckey suggested that offshore facilities could provide access to medical treatments currently prohibited in the United States. That raises difficult questions about patient safety and whether those activities could legally take place offshore.
Luckey says he and several close friends funded SLAB at a $1 billion valuation back in 2017. However, that figure refers to the project's reported valuation at the time. It does not establish that $1 billion has been spent building it. He also says the project has made significant progress, although considerable work remains. So far, he has not publicly disclosed a confirmed construction schedule or a precise location for the proposed platform.
Interestingly, Luckey only decided to discuss SLAB publicly after learning that journalists were preparing to describe it as a floating AI data center. He pushed back on that description, saying the project was much older and considerably more ambitious. His comments suggest that data centers could be part of the broader concept, but SLAB was conceived for other industrial activities as well.
This is where Luckey's proposal runs into some complicated legal questions. According to the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management, most coastal states, including California, have jurisdiction over submerged lands extending approximately three nautical miles offshore. Beyond that boundary, federal authority becomes especially important. The United States has a territorial sea extending 12 nautical miles from its coastal baselines. It also maintains an exclusive economic zone extending up to 200 nautical miles offshore.
The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration explains that the federal government retains authority over certain offshore structures and activities within that zone. Consequently, moving a business beyond California's coastal boundary would not automatically eliminate federal oversight. Environmental requirements and maritime regulations could still apply. The legal picture would also depend on whether SLAB floats freely, anchors to the ocean floor or operates under a particular country's registration. Luckey has yet to explain exactly how the platform would navigate those requirements.
Building a permanent industrial community offshore presents extraordinary engineering challenges. Saltwater gradually corrodes exposed structures, and powerful storms can place enormous stress on offshore installations. Maintaining a facility for centuries would require substantial engineering and ongoing repairs. Then there is the expense of running an industrial operation at sea. Workers would need transportation to the platform, while supplies and equipment would have to travel across the water.
That makes Luckey's goal of operating more cheaply than comparable land-based facilities particularly ambitious. A 1,000-year design life is also a target rather than a demonstrated lifespan. Until Luckey releases detailed engineering evidence, there is no way to independently verify whether SLAB could meet that goal.
California has long been associated with technological innovation, yet it also has extensive environmental and land-use regulations. Some businesses argue that permitting requirements make industrial development more expensive and time-consuming. Luckey's proposal brings that debate into focus. Moving industrial activity offshore would be a drastic response to regulatory frustration. However, the idea also raises a question worth asking: Have some regulations become so burdensome that entrepreneurs would rather build at sea than navigate the approval process on land?
Of course, industries involving hazardous chemicals or experimental medical treatments require serious oversight. Those protections help prevent accidents and protect public health. At the same time, regulations can become unnecessarily complicated or outdated. Governments need to examine whether their approval processes encourage responsible innovation or create obstacles that serve little practical purpose. Luckey has not identified the specific California laws he hopes to avoid. For now, his project highlights a broader argument about how America regulates industrial development. Whether SLAB becomes a functioning offshore community remains to be seen.
I find the whole idea fascinating, but something about it also strikes me as completely absurd. Have we really reached a point where building a giant industrial platform in the ocean sounds more appealing than dealing with government regulations on land? California, in particular, should be paying attention. This is a state that helped create Silicon Valley, yet we're now talking about taking American industry offshore to escape regulatory headaches. I'm certainly not suggesting we eliminate important environmental or safety protections. But there's a point where excessive regulation can start working against the very innovation we should be encouraging. I'd much rather see American businesses building here, creating jobs and developing new technology without unnecessary roadblocks. Luckey still has a tremendous amount to prove before SLAB becomes reality. But the fact that he's seriously pursuing this idea should give policymakers something to think about. For more on this story and our discussion about the future of American innovation, listen to The CyberGuy Report Podcast at cyberguy.com/podcast/.
Would you support American companies moving industrial operations offshore to avoid certain regulations, or should lawmakers focus on reforming those regulations here at home? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com

articles.title: Floral tributes moved to make space
articles.excerpt: The Hong Kong Special Administrative Region Government announced today that floral tributes placed in remembrance of the Wang Fuk Court…
articles.fullText:
The Hong Kong Special Administrative Region Government announced today that floral tributes placed in remembrance of the Wang Fuk Court fire have been temporarily moved to a nearby lawn so members of the public can continue laying flowers.

According to the Government, many bouquets have been spontaneously placed near Wang Fuk Court in Tai Po to mourn the victims.

Anticipating larger crowds in the evening, authorities carefully packed some bouquets and mourning items into plastic boxes and relocated them to an adjacent lawn. This frees up space for arriving visitors to pay their respects while ensuring every gesture of goodwill is treated with dignity.

To manage the growing volume of tributes, the Government will progressively transfer the items to religious venues. This arrangement will properly preserve the public’s condolences across the community, make room for further tributes, and keep the site clean and orderly.

articles.title: FS begins visit to the Netherlands
articles.excerpt: Financial Secretary Paul Chan, leading a Hong Kong business and innovation and technology (I&T) delegation, began his visit to the…
articles.fullText:
Financial Secretary Paul Chan, leading a Hong Kong business and innovation and technology (I&T) delegation, began his visit to the Netherlands yesterday after concluding a trip to the UK.

Upon arriving in The Hague, Mr Chan met Secretary-General of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Netherlands Christiaan Rebergen to discuss the “one country, two systems” framework, Hong Kong’s business environment, its latest economic and financial situation and ways to deepen bilateral co-operation.

Mr Chan noted that the delegation’s visit aims to showcase Hong Kong’s latest developments and promote new opportunities in finance, investment, I&T and the Northern Metropolis to Dutch sectors, fostering closer ties between both sides.

He also met Treasurer-General of the Ministry of Finance of the Netherlands Jasper Wesseling for an in-depth exchange on economic and capital market developments in the Netherlands and across Europe. During the meeting, Mr Chan briefed him on Hong Kong’s latest financial market progress and policies to advance I&T industries, particularly measures aimed at attracting strategic enterprises to establish operations in the city.

In addition, Mr Chan met representatives of the Netherlands Institute of International Relations, briefing them on Hong Kong’s latest outlook and exchanging views on China’s economic development and the international landscape.

Later that day, he called on Chinese Ambassador to the Netherlands Shen Bo to discuss China-Netherlands relations and further scope for co-operation between Hong Kong and the Netherlands.

articles.title: Ride-hailing permits open Nov 30
articles.excerpt: The Transport Department (TD) announced that applications for a ride-hailing vehicle driving permit will open at 10am on November 30…
articles.fullText:
The Transport Department (TD) announced that applications for a ride-hailing vehicle driving permit will open at 10am on November 30.

Outlining the arrangements today, the TD said there is no quota on these permits, and applications will be accepted all year round.

Applicants must fulfil the related statutory requirements, including being at least 21 years old on the application date, and holding a Hong Kong Permanent Identity Card, or an Identity Card without any condition of stay other than a limit of stay.

They must also have held a valid full driving licence for a private car or light goods vehicle for at least one year, and have no serious traffic convictions specified in the law within five years prior to the application date.

The law also stipulates that the applicants must have passed the taxi and ride-hailing vehicle combined written test, and have completed a pre-service course for ride-hailing vehicle drivers.

The TD launched the combined written test on August 3, while 11 designated pre-service training schools began offering a pre-service course for ride-hailing vehicle drivers in October so applicants can register for both.

Individuals holding a valid taxi driving licence may apply for a driving permit directly, without having to retake the combined written test or complete the pre-service course.

Eligible applicants may submit online applications through GovHK anytime starting at 10am on November 30.

Click here for details and call the hotline at 2804 2600 for enquiries.

Regarding vehicle permits, the TD said the legislation caps the number issued at 10,000. If valid applications for vehicle permits exceed this prescribed limit, permits will be allocated by drawing lots.

The TD plans to invite applications for these permits in early 2027, with specific arrangements to be announced in due course.

articles.title: China, HK stocks end the day with losses
articles.excerpt: Stocks on the mainland and in Hong Kong ended lower on Wednesday, with the Shanghai benchmark logging its steepest one-day…
articles.fullText:
Stocks on the mainland and in Hong Kong ended lower on Wednesday, with the Shanghai benchmark logging its steepest one-day decline in three months, pressured by overnight losses on Wall Street and weakness across regional peers.

By the close, the benchmark Shanghai Composite dropped two percent to its lowest closing level since July 2025.

The blue-chip CSI300 index fell 1.7 percent to book its softest close in more than 17 months.

In Hong Kong, the stock market ended lower, with the benchmark Hang Seng Index down 1.14 percent to close at 21,966 points.

The Hang Seng China Enterprises Index retreated 0.91 percent, and the Hang Seng Tech Index shed 2.56 percent.

Meanwhile, the Trump administration is poised to imminently release the findings of
a probe aimed at countering alleged excess industrial capacity in 16 major US trading partners.

Media reports say the probe could recommend a new round of import duties on a wide range of goods from trading partners such as China, the European Union, Japan, and South Korea.

"Even if the overall tariff rates remain within previously negotiated limits, changes to product coverage and exemptions could have significant implications for individual industries and regional supply chains," Commerzbank analysts said in a note.

Beijing urged the United States on Wednesday to "uphold the stable development" of trade relations, following reports about a potential new round of tariffs from Washington.

"Tariff wars and trade wars are not in anyone's interest," Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said, when asked about Washington's reported plans.

Guo added the world's two top economies, which in 2025 agreed a truce in their trade dispute, "should resolve relevant issues through consultation".

articles.title: China, Pakistan exchange Shenzhou-24 congratulations
articles.excerpt: President Xi Jinping and his Pakistani counterpart Asif Ali Zardari have exchanged congratulations on the joint spaceflight mission carried out…
articles.fullText:
President Xi Jinping and his Pakistani counterpart Asif Ali Zardari have exchanged congratulations on the joint spaceflight mission carried out by astronauts from the two countries.

China's Shenzhou-24 spacecraft successfully blasted off on Wednesday morning, carrying two Chinese astronauts Tang Hongbo and Wu Yi, along with Muhammad Zeeshan Ali from Pakistan, to Tiangong space station.

Ali is the first foreign astronaut to board the space station.

In his message, Xi said the joint space exploration of astronauts from China and Pakistan is a vivid embodiment of the deep-rooted friendship between the two countries, as well as another important achievement in bilateral cooperation, according to Xinhua News Agency.

The president said China stands ready to work with Pakistan and other countries to champion the peaceful use of outer space and deepen space cooperation.

The Shenzhou-24 spaceship docked with the Tiangong space station more than three hours after it blasted off.

The crew later entered the space station.

Edited by Edmond Fong

articles.title: China pushes sovereignty claims through patriotic cruises to disputed Paracel Islands
articles.excerpt: Soft power play in South China Sea comes as rival claimant Vietnam seeks closer ties with China.
articles.fullText:
Read a version of this story in Vietnamese .
China’s “patriotic” tourist cruises to the disputed Paracel Islands in the South China Sea are a calculated move by Beijing to normalize its de facto control over the islands through soft power and collective memory, an expert from Vietnam – a country which also claims the Paracels – told Radio Free Asia.
The latest assertion of Chinese sovereignty comes at a time when Hanoi seeks to maintain stable ties with Beijing, without ceding ground on its own claims.
The revamped cruise program, launched in early October, features a theatrical production depicting generations of Chinese fishermen defending what Beijing considers its maritime territory, alongside other activities promoting national identity and territorial sovereignty.
China has controlled the entire Paracel archipelago since 1974 – at the tail end of the Vietnam War – when it seized the remaining islands held by South Vietnam following a naval clash. Vietnam and Taiwan also claim the islands, which lie between the Vietnamese coast and China’s southern island province of Hainan.
The Paracel Islands in the disputed South China Sea. Credit: RFA
Hanoi’s current pursuit of maritime cooperation with Beijing makes it difficult for Vietnam to protest China’s soft power moves, but doing nothing only helps Beijing, an expert from Vietnam told RFA Vietnamese on condition of anonymity for security reasons.
“If Hanoi simply maintains a calm posture to preserve diplomatic momentum without taking timely legal action in response to each incremental infringement, Beijing could easily exploit that silence to gradually lower the threshold for resistance across the region,” the expert said.
From sightseeing to sovereignty
China has operated tourist cruises to the Paracels since 2013, but the latest initiative places a greater emphasis on patriotic education, incorporating political messages into entertainment and recreational activities throughout the voyage.
Hainan Port and Shipping Holding Co., in cooperation with the Hainan Performing Arts Group, launched an upgraded service aboard the cruise ship Xianglong Dao on Oct. 3, according to a Xinhua Finance report republished by Sina Finance.
The four-day cruise departs from Sanya in Hainan province and travels to Tree Island, known in China as Zhaoshu Island, in the northern part of the Paracel archipelago.
Marketed under the slogan “ One trip to Xisha, a lifetime of love for the motherland ,” the program features three consecutive evenings of performances, including an original theatrical production titled “Defending the Ancestral Sea.”
The play depicts generations of fishermen from Tanmen, a fishing community in Hainan, making a living at sea and “protecting the blue frontier.” Other activities include performances of revolutionary songs and live dubbing of patriotic films – a type of performance art in China during which old films are played without their audio tracks and live actors voice all the spoken lines.
Upon arriving at Tree Island, passengers participate in Chinese flag-raising ceremonies, patriotic education sessions and beach cleanups.
Soldiers of China's People's Liberation Army Navy patrol at Woody Island, in the disputed Paracel Archipelago, January 29, 2016.
(Reuters) Xianglong Dao completed eight voyages in the first month of the revamped service, recording 2,516 attendances at its performances, according to figures released by the operator and published by Chinese news portal Sohu on Nov. 5.
The tourism program complements Beijing’s broader efforts to consolidate its administrative and civilian presence in disputed waters. In 2012, China established Sansha, a city headquartered on Woody Island in the Paracels, to administer vast areas of the South China Sea it claims as its territory.
Maritime negotiations stall
During the ASEAN summit in Manila last week, Southeast Asian countries again failed to reach an agreement with China on rules governing conduct in the South China Sea, a strategically important waterway through which trillions of dollars in global trade pass annually.
China claims most of the sea, overlapping with maritime and territorial claims by Vietnam, the Philippines, Malaysia, Brunei and Taiwan.
In 2016, an international arbitral tribunal in The Hague ruled that China’s claims to historic rights over resources within its so-called nine-dash line had no legal basis. Beijing has rejected the ruling.
ASEAN and China have been working toward a code of conduct for years following the signing of a nonbinding declaration in 2002, and leading up to this year’s summit, the regional bloc had a goal of finalizing the code in 2026, but differences over the proposed agreement’s scope and enforceability have hampered progress.
Anti-China protester Le Hoang (R) joins fellow protesters as they hold a banner and chant anti-China slogans during a gathering to mark the 40th anniversary of the Chinese occupation of the disputed Paracels islands in the South China Sea, in Hanoi, January 19, 2014.
(Reuters) ASEAN Secretary-General Kao Kim Hourn said on Nov. 18 that more than 80% of the text of the code of conduct had been completed, with the remaining provisions expected to be negotiated in 2027.
Key issues, including whether the agreement would be legally binding and which geographical areas it would cover, remain unresolved.
Hanoi walks a diplomatic tightrope
Vietnam, which has long sought to balance its economic and political ties with China against its territorial disputes with Beijing, has continued to emphasize bilateral cooperation.
China is Vietnam’s largest trading partner, and the two countries maintain close ties between their ruling communist parties despite longstanding tensions over the South China Sea.
A review of public statements issued by Vietnam’s Foreign Ministry in October and November found no specific condemnation of the revamped cruise program.
Hanoi’s most recently identified statement on the Paracels was issued on Aug. 28, when it denounced Chinese construction activities at two maritime features in the archipelago as illegal.
Ahead of this month’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, Vietnamese Communist Party General Secretary and President To Lam published an article titled “One ocean, one future” in the state-run China Daily, highlighting the importance of regional maritime cooperation.
China's President Xi Jinping, right, shakes hands with Vietnam's President To Lam before leaders take a group photo during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit in Shenzhen, China, Nov. 19, 2026.
(Greg Baker/AFP) On Nov. 22, two Vietnamese coast guard vessels departed the northern port city of Hai Phong for a joint patrol with their Chinese counterparts along the maritime boundary in the Gulf of Tonkin, Vietnamese newspaper Tuoi Tre reported .
The patrol, the second this year, covers 262 nautical miles (485 kilometers). Unlike the disputed waters surrounding the Paracels, the Gulf of Tonkin is subject to a maritime boundary agreement signed by Vietnam and China in 2000.
The Vietnamese expert warned, however, that cooperation in areas where maritime boundaries had been settled should not overshadow Beijing’s efforts to consolidate its control elsewhere.
“In the long run, stability at diplomatic receptions or in demarcated waters such as the Gulf of Tonkin cannot obscure the reality that sovereignty over the Paracel Islands is being eroded day by day through civilian means,” the expert said.
Edited by Taejun Kang and Eugene Whong.

articles.title: Shenzhou-24 docks with Tiangong space station
articles.excerpt: The Shenzhou-24 crewed spaceship successfully docked with the Tiangong space station at 11.56am on Wednesday, according to the China Manned…
articles.fullText:
The Shenzhou-24 crewed spaceship successfully docked with the Tiangong space station at 11.56am on Wednesday, according to the China Manned Space Agency (CMSA).

The spaceship made a fast, automated rendezvous and docking with the front port of Tiangong's core module Tianhe.

The whole docking process took approximately 3.5 hours, said the CMSA.

The astronaut trio aboard the spaceship – Chinese astronauts Tang Hongbo, Wu Yi and Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, the first foreigner to visit Tiangong – will then enter the Tianhe module.

The Shenzhou-23 crew members in the space station are ready to receive the new arrivals.

The Shenzhou-24 spaceship, atop a Long March-2F carrier rocket, blasted off at 8.18am from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwest China on Wednesday. The CMSA described the launch as "a complete success". (Xinhua)

Edited by Edmond Fong

articles.title: 'HK backs advancement of digital tech in global trade'
articles.excerpt: Director-General of Trade and Industry Aaron Liu on Wednesday said Hong Kong fully backs the advancement of digital technologies in…
articles.fullText:
Director-General of Trade and Industry Aaron Liu on Wednesday said Hong Kong fully backs the advancement of digital technologies in international trade.

Speaking on an RTHK programme, he noted that the Apec Trade Digitalisation Cooperation Framework – a four-year regional initiative – was adopted by the 21 member economies at last week’s Apec meetings in Shenzhen.

“We will fully support the recently endorsed Apec Trade Digitalisation Cooperation Framework. We will continue to make good use of the Apec platform to share Hong Kong’s experience as an international trade centre and in digital trade, telling the good stories of Hong Kong,” Liu said.

“For example, when we attended an Apec event in Dalian in August, our department held two workshops on digital service trade rules and data standards, inviting relevant experts and industry representatives to share our experience and exchange ideas.”

Pointing out that Hong Kong plays a unique role by participating in Apec both as a member economy and a special administrative region of China, Liu said the SAR not only keeps abreast of the latest international trends, but also takes part in formulating cooperation directions on emerging topics such as digital trade and the green economy.

He also noted that Hong Kong, leveraging its unique advantages of the motherland’s support and being closely connected to the world under the One Country, Two Systems principle, achieved positive outcomes during the Apec China year which saw the country host a year-long series of Apec events.

Moving forward, Liu said the SAR will continue to actively participate in Apec affairs, leveraging its strengths as a “super connector” and “super value-adder” to contribute to national development.

Edited by Edmond Fong

articles.title: Local blue chips buck regional sell-off
articles.excerpt: Hong Kong stocks rose at the open of trade on Wednesday despite a regional sell-off triggered by fresh US tariff…
articles.fullText:
Hong Kong stocks rose at the open of trade on Wednesday despite a regional sell-off triggered by fresh US tariff threats and as tech-led rally fizzled.

The benchmark Hang Seng Index gained 33 points, or 0.15 percent, to open at 22,252.81 points.

Mainland stock markets opened lower, with the benchmark Shanghai Composite Index down 0.73 percent to open at 3,522 points.

The Shenzhen Component Index opened 1.45 percent lower at 10,272 points.

The STAR Composite Index, which reflects the performance of stocks on China's sci-tech innovation board, opened 2.2 percent lower at 1,369 points.

Japanese and South Korean stocks dived in morning trade as the euphoria sparked by Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia faded amid lingering questions over the AI boom.

The Nikkei 225 stock index sank 3.1 percent while South Korea's Kospi shed 4.8 percent.

Both markets had surged on Tuesday.

Risk appetite weakened after media reports the Trump administration was preparing to release findings of a trade investigation that could pave the way for new tariff measures. (Agencies)

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: China successfully launches Shenzhou-24 spaceship
articles.excerpt: The China Manned Space Agency (CMSA) said on Wednesday that the launch of the Shenzhou-24 crewed spaceship was "a complete…
articles.fullText:
The China Manned Space Agency (CMSA) said on Wednesday that the launch of the Shenzhou-24 crewed spaceship was "a complete success".

The spaceship, atop a Long March-2F carrier rocket, blasted off at 8.18am from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwest China, sending Chinese astronauts Tang Hongbo, Wu Yi and Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali to China's orbiting Tiangong space station, according to the CMSA.

About 10 minutes after the launch, the spaceship separated from the rocket and entered its designated orbit, the CMSA said, adding that the astronauts are in good condition.

The spaceship will later perform a fast, automated rendezvous and docking with the space station complex, and the Shenzhou-24 crew will then enter Tiangong.

The Shenzhou-24 mission marks the first joint flight consisting of Chinese and foreign astronauts in the history of China's manned space programme.

Zeeshan Ali, a 40-year-old pilot who will become the first Pakistani in orbit, will work as a payload specialist and is set to stay at the station for five to 10 days, conducting experiments.

To prepare for the flight, Ali trained for seven months in Beijing, during which he underwent intensive Chinese-language classes, learning Chinese songs and reading Chinese poetry. He also practised calligraphy and played table tennis.

"I'm not flying for myself. I carry the name of Pakistan on my shoulder," Ali told reporters on Tuesday. (Xinhua/Reuters)

articles.title: Sinner doubtful for Australian Open after knee surgery
articles.excerpt: World number two Jannik Sinner is at risk of missing the 2027 Australian Open after undergoing knee surgery, Italian media…
articles.fullText:
World number two Jannik Sinner is at risk of missing the 2027 Australian Open after undergoing knee surgery, Italian media reported on Tuesday.

According to television channels Rai and Sky Sport as well as newspaper La Gazzetta dello Sport, the 25-year-old could be out for three months.

Next year's opening Grand Slam tournament in Melbourne, where Sinner is a two-time champion, starts on January 17.

Sinner's doctor, Herbert Schoenhuber, told Rai the surgery in Finland went well but his press officer has yet to reply to AFP's request for comment.

The five-time Grand Slam winner has been sidelined since claiming his maiden Wimbledon title in July and has since lost his world-number-one ranking to Alexander Zverev.

Sinner met with a host of specialists before announcing the end of his season in October.

"The worst part of this injury for me is that I can't compete, I can't play tennis," Sinner said in a recent documentary.

"Even my life outside tennis is a bit more limited, for the simple reason that I can't do the things I really love, because I want to protect my knee as much as possible." (AFP)

Edited by Cecil Wong

articles.title: City, Arsenal draw in Champions League as Real cruise
articles.excerpt: Rayan Cherki's late equaliser saved Manchester City from defeat to Napoli but a 2-2 draw on Tuesday did little to…
articles.fullText:
Rayan Cherki's late equaliser saved Manchester City from defeat to Napoli but a 2-2 draw on Tuesday did little to expel the gloom hanging over the English giants on and off the field.

Cherki's fine individual strike four minutes from time denied Napoli a first ever win on English soil after they twice went in front in the second half through Rasmus Hojlund and Noa Lang.

But City have won just once from open play in seven matches in all competitions as uncertainty over the club's future seeps into their performances on the pitch.

City won 10 of their first 11 games in all competitions under Enzo Maresca. But the wheels have come off in the wake of the club being found guilty for widespread breaches of Premier League financial rules.

The 10-time English champions face a severe points deduction, or even relegation from the Premier League, unless they can overturn the ruling on appeal.

Not since 2008, prior to an Adu Dhabi-backed takeover that transformed the club's fortunes, have City failed to win in four consecutive home games.

"We don't like these moments. We want to win games, but unfortunately this moment is like this," said Maresca, ahead of a trip to Premier League champions Arsenal on Sunday.

"In this moment it's clear that we are conceding too many goals. We need to adjust and we are able to."

At the Emirates, Arsenal striker Viktor Gyokeres showed why he is such a polarising figure with a thunderous goal and a crucial miss in his side's 1-1 draw against Borussia Dortmund.

Gunners boss Mikel Arteta had urged Gyokeres to seize his opportunity after selecting the Sweden striker instead of Kai Havertz for the league phase tie at the Emirates Stadium.

Initially, Gyokeres looked like doing just that with his first goal at the Emirates Stadium this season, and only his third for the Gunners in all competitions.

But the 28-year-old has been much-maligned for his erratic displays since arriving from Sporting Lisbon in 2025.

And he gave more ammunition to his critics when he missed a golden opportunity to seal the points with a woeful header in the closing stages.

Dortmund had equalised through Maximilian Beier by then and Arteta was left to rue his decision to put his faith in Gyokeres.

Arsenal are unbeaten in their last 11 games in all competitions, but this was not a vintage display by the English champions, who failed to win at home for the first time this season.

Arsenal sit fifth in the league phase with three wins and two draws from their five matches, while seventh-placed Dortmund are one point behind them.

Real Madrid, meanwhile, continued their 100 percent start in Europe after coming from behind to thrash PSV 5-1.

PSV put up an impressive fight in the first half but Jose Mourinho's side blew them away with a dynamic showing in the second, inspired by England midfielder Jude Bellingham. (AFP)

Edited by Cecil Wong

articles.title: Senegal regain Afcon title after appeal to Cas
articles.excerpt: Senegal on Tuesday regained their Africa Cup of Nations title after winning an appeal to the Court of Arbitration for…
articles.fullText:
Senegal on Tuesday regained their Africa Cup of Nations title after winning an appeal to the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas) against the decision by the Confederation of African Football to declare Morocco the winners following a chaotic final in January.

"The Court of Arbitration for Sport has upheld the appeal by the Senegalese Football Federation (FSF) against the Confederation of African Football (Caf) and the Royal Moroccan Football Federation (FRMF) concerning the final of the Africa Cup of Nations Morocco 2025," Cas said in a statement.

The Swiss-based sports court said Senegal's appeal had been upheld by "a unanimous decision," and their original 1-0 victory after extra time is reinstated.

In March, the Confederation of African Football (Caf) sensationally overturned the result of the final, awarding Morocco a 3-0 victory, and the title, after many Senegalese players walked off the pitch in protest at a penalty given to the hosts with the game still goalless.

The Caf Appeals Committee had justified its decision to overturn the result and declare Morocco champions based on Articles 82 and 84 of the Afcon Regulations.

Those state that if a team "refuses to play or leaves the ground before the regular end of the match without the authorisation of the referee, it shall be considered (loser) and shall be eliminated for good from the current competition."

However, the Senegal players eventually returned to the pitch and the final carried on.

The Cas panel therefore considered that the referee's decision to restart the final showed that "the conditions for resuming the match had been met," and that articles 82 and 84 were therefore "not applicable in this case." (AFP)

Edited by Cecil Wong

articles.title: Nvidia, Anthropic head south as AI shares fall
articles.excerpt: The Nasdaq and the S&P 500 closed lower on Tuesday as Nvidia and other AI-related shares gave back some of…
articles.fullText:
The Nasdaq and the S&P 500 closed lower on Tuesday as Nvidia and other AI-related shares gave back some of the previous day's sharp gains and investors braced for possible new tariffs.

Nvidia's stock slipped 5.9 percent as investors weighed the implications of Jensen Huang's reinstatement as CEO on Monday following questions about the political and governance risks surrounding his return. Technology fell 2.8 percent, leading sector declines in the S&P 500, while an index of semiconductors dropped 7.9 percent.

Nvidia's decision to bring back Huang drove a sharp rally in its stock and the market on Monday, giving the S&P 500 and Nasdaq their biggest daily percentage gains since April 2025.

Reuters reported, citing three people with knowledge of the matter, that the Trump administration is poised to imminently release the findings of a probe aimed at countering alleged excess industrial capacity in 16 major US trading partners, and that new import duties on a wide range of goods are expected.

"After the biggest rally in months, you would expect some profit-taking. At the end of the day, one headline doesn't really resolve investor questions about the AI trade," said Gene Goldman, chief investment officer at Cetera Financial Group.

"The correction that we had last week is a buying opportunity for long-term investors, but we continue to believe it can be a very bumpy path for some time," Goldman said.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 423.39 points, or 0.9 percent, to 50,018.70, the S&P 500 lost 36.08 points, or 0.5 percent, to 7,201.09 and the Nasdaq Composite lost 356.02 points, or 1.5 percent, to 23,733.54.

Before Monday's rebound, AI-linked stocks had struggled for weeks as investors questioned the sector's debt-fuelled spending and the returns it could generate.

Anthropic's shares ended 6.5 percent lower at US$81.90, below their US$83 IPO price. The AI startup had a blockbuster market debut last week.

Additional tariffs would add uncertainty to the market, while investors were also cautious ahead of Wednesday's Personal Consumption Expenditures report, Goldman said.

The administration's tariffs have contributed to higher prices on consumer goods in the United States.

The PCE price index is one of the key inflation gauges watched by the Federal Reserve. Fed funds futures traders are pricing in 97 percent odds of a Fed hike in December, and a 66 percent chance of an additional increase in January, according to the CME Group's FedWatch Tool.

Retailers were among the day's gainers. Shares of Abercrombie & Fitch, which raised its profit forecast, jumped 19.7 percent, while Dollar Tree gained 11.2 percent, also after raising its profit outlook.

Earlier, a Conference Board survey showed US consumer confidence rose to its highest level in nearly two years in November amid optimism over the labour market and the economy following this month's midterm elections. (Reuters)

Edited by Cecil Wong

articles.title: US consumer confidence soars as petrol prices decline
articles.excerpt: Americans’ confidence in the economy jumped this month as petrol prices continued their steady decline and election-related uncertainty ended. The…
articles.fullText:
Americans’ confidence in the economy jumped this month as petrol prices continued their steady decline and election-related uncertainty ended.

The US Conference Board said on Tuesday that its consumer confidence index soared to 103.3 this month, from a reading of 91.9 in October. It’s the second straight increase after the index fell in September to its lowest level since April 2014, even lower than during the pandemic.

Consumer confidence is closely linked to petrol prices, and the Conference Board also said Americans see the job market improving. The increase also reflected sharp political divisions, as confidence rose sharply for Democrats and independents, while it declined modestly for Republicans.

The improvement could signal a pick-up in consumer spending in the months ahead, though Americans have been spending at a solid pace this year even as consumer surveys have been lacklustre. Economists say the surveys are not as reliable a measure of consumers' behaviour as they have been in the past.

Still, the increase could be a good sign for retailers as winter holiday shopping gets underway. The National Retail Federation has forecast sales will rise at a healthy clip over the holidays despite stubbornly high inflation, which is rising faster than average weekly pay cheques.

Separately, petrol prices have continued to quickly decline, though they remain higher than they usually are at this time of year, when prices typically fall.

Prices at the pump fell to US$3.61 a gallon on average nationwide on Tuesday, according to the American Automobile Association, down 17 cents from a week ago and sharply below the average of US$4.30 a month earlier. Still, prices remain well above the US$3.07 that motorists were paying at this time last year. (AP)

Edited by Cecil Wong

articles.title: What United Airlines banning AI agents from booking flights means for your travel plans
articles.excerpt: United Airlines is blocking unauthorized AI travel agents from its booking systems, warning that automated purchases could put MileagePlus miles…
articles.fullText:
Wouldn't it be nice to tell an AI assistant to find the cheapest flight to your destination and book your favorite seat while you do something else? That kind of convenience is getting closer. But United Airlines wants to make sure an unauthorized AI assistant never gets that far.
The airline is restricting third-party AI agents from accessing its booking systems without permission. United says these tools could expose sensitive customer information and make purchases travelers never intended to authorize. The concern also extends to MileagePlus accounts, where an automated mistake could put valuable airline miles at risk.
The decision comes as AI assistants become increasingly capable of taking action on our behalf. While that sounds convenient, United is raising questions about how much control we should give software over our travel plans. Here's where United draws the line and what you need to know before letting AI handle your next flight booking.

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
FORMER ANTHROPIC SECURITY LEADER WARNS AI AGENTS ARE BECOMING TOO AUTONOMOUS FOR HUMANS TO KEEP THEM IN CHECK
On Nov. 11, United Airlines published an official news release titled United Restricts Access for Third-Party AI Agents. The airline explained that protecting customer information and account security prompted the restrictions. According to United, sharing account credentials with personal AI assistants can expose sensitive information. The airline also warned that automated actions might lead to unwanted purchases or changes to existing reservations. Then there's the issue of frequent flyer miles. United specifically mentioned the possibility that an AI assistant could use MileagePlus miles without the traveler intending that redemption.
To address those concerns, United is restricting unauthorized personal AI agents from accessing its digital platforms. The rules also reach travel agencies and booking services that might use automated AI tools to access United's systems. United says it is updating its policies to support these restrictions. The airline also plans to continue evaluating how personal AI assistants interact with its services.
You may already use AI to research vacation destinations or figure out which airport is closest to your hotel. An AI travel agent takes that technology further by performing tasks for you. For example, you could ask an AI assistant to find a flight under $400 that arrives before dinner. Instead of simply recommending flights, an AI agent might search booking systems and attempt to complete the reservation. Some agents can also interact with websites using a browser. That means they may be able to enter personal information and complete steps that normally require you to click through a booking process.
The convenience is easy to understand. However, granting an AI assistant access to your airline account can also give it the ability to make changes you never intended. For more on what these assistants can do, see our article on eight seriously annoying tasks you can hand off to an AI agent.
United's concerns go beyond account security. The airline also warns that automated AI activity could potentially violate Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and Department of Transportation (DOT) regulations. Consider what happens when you check in for a flight. Airlines require travelers to acknowledge important safety information, including whether their bags contain prohibited hazardous materials.
United specifically points to the requirement for a person to confirm that baggage contains no banned substances, such as explosives. An AI assistant handling check-in could potentially bypass that acknowledgment. After all, how would an AI assistant know what you actually packed in your suitcase? United has identified this as a potential regulatory concern. The airline has not established that every AI-assisted check-in violates federal law.
This may be the biggest concern for travelers experimenting with automated booking tools. United revised its Contract of Carriage on Nov. 11. The updated rules prohibit AI agents from making or modifying tickets and purchasing airline products or services.
The contract also identifies reservations made or changed through AI agents as subject to cancellation without advance notice. The definition of an AI agent includes automated tools even when a traveler supervises or approves their actions. However, there is an important exception for existing reservations.
United says bookings made by AI agents before Nov. 11, will not be canceled under the new restriction. The airline recommends reviewing those reservations to confirm that they were properly booked and ticketed. If you previously used an AI assistant to arrange United travel, open the United app or website and verify your itinerary. Check that your ticket was actually issued rather than assuming a booking confirmation means everything is complete. You can review the airline's published rules in its Contract of Carriage at united.com/en/us/fly/contract-of-carriage.html .
MALICIOUS BROWSER EXTENSIONS CAN HIJACK AI ASSISTANTS
Yes, although United has established limits on how outside AI tools can interact with its systems. You can still ask an AI chatbot for general travel advice or help creating an itinerary. United's guidance allows AI-assisted research and trip planning as long as the tool does not access United's website or app. However, an unauthorized AI agent cannot search United's website or app on your behalf. The restriction also covers automated purchasing and reservation management. That means an AI-powered browser feature that automatically searches United's website could fall under the restriction, even if it never buys a ticket.
United says assistive technology for travelers with disabilities remains unaffected. Traditional travel booking services can also continue operating through permitted channels. The restriction specifically addresses unauthorized AI agents, including those used by travel agencies. According to United's published guidance, the airline does not currently work with any third-party AI agents under this policy.
While United is putting restrictions in place, Southwest Airlines is exploring a different approach. On Oct. 6, Southwest announced a ChatGPT integration. The feature allows you to discover destinations and shop for Southwest flights directly through ChatGPT. However, Southwest's integration still directs you to the airline's website to complete purchases. The company describes the arrangement as an early step toward broader AI-powered booking capabilities.
That approach gives Southwest a way to use AI for flight discovery while maintaining control over the final transaction. United is taking a more restrictive position on outside AI assistants. The airline says it will continue evaluating the technology as it develops.
If you normally book flights through United's website or app, you can continue doing so. You can also use permitted travel booking services. However, if you've started experimenting with AI assistants that make purchases or manage accounts on your behalf, United's restrictions deserve your attention. An AI agent with access to your airline account could potentially reach sensitive travel information. Depending on its permissions, it might also make purchases you never intended to authorize. Here are a few ways to protect yourself.
Avoid giving third-party AI assistants your MileagePlus password or other sensitive login information. If you've already shared your credentials with an AI agent, United recommends changing your password immediately. You should also remove any saved login details from the AI service. Consider using a password manager to create and securely store a strong, unique password for your airline account. This can help protect your account if a password you use elsewhere gets exposed in a data breach.
Strong antivirus software can help protect your devices from malware and malicious links designed to steal login credentials . This is especially important if you use travel booking websites or receive airline confirmation emails. While antivirus protection won't stop an AI assistant from making an unauthorized reservation, it can help prevent cybercriminals from gaining access to your MileagePlus account. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.
Use United's official website or app, or a booking provider operating under United's rules. United currently does not work with third-party AI agents under this policy. Even if an AI assistant offers to complete a reservation with your approval, that does not necessarily make the transaction permissible.
UNITED AIRLINES SAYS TECHNOLOGY ISSUE RESOLVED AFTER ‘WIDESPREAD SYSTEM OUTAGE’
Review your MileagePlus balance for unexpected activity. If you notice a redemption or purchase you don't recognize, secure your account immediately. Contact United through its official website or app to report the activity and request assistance.
Check your booking confirmation and make sure United has issued your ticket. If an AI assistant arranged your travel before Nov. 11, verify the reservation directly with the airline. United says those earlier bookings will not be canceled under the new restriction.
AI can still help you plan a trip using general information without accessing United's systems. However, complete your flight purchases and reservation changes yourself through permitted channels. That way, you can review what you're buying without risking a prohibited AI-agent transaction.
I can see why United is concerned. I've spent enough time searching for flights to appreciate the idea of handing that job over to AI. Let the assistant find me a great fare and save me the hassle of comparing a dozen options. I'm all for that. But the moment it starts making purchases or accessing my airline miles, I want to know exactly what it's doing.
I recently spoke with travel expert Katy Nastro, who discovered that someone had stolen 50,000 miles from her American Airlines account. Her experience had nothing to do with AI agents, but it reminded me how much value we keep in these loyalty programs. I certainly wouldn't want an automated mistake putting those rewards at risk.
At the same time, I do wonder whether security is the only concern driving United's decision. Airlines have spent years building direct relationships with travelers. AI agents could change how we compare fares and choose which airline gets our business. I would hate to see useful technology held back simply because it gives you more control over the shopping process. United says it will keep evaluating these tools, and I hope that eventually leads to a secure way to book flights using AI. Until then, I'm happy to let AI help find my next trip. I'll take care of the booking myself.
