US President Donald Trump praised Shenzhen as "immaculate" while contrasting the metropolis to the conditions of American cities during a White House news conference.

Speaking shortly after returning to Washington, DC, from the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit, he noted the city's growth from a fishing village not long ago, crediting President Xi Jinping for the development.

"What a job President Xi has done, it's clean it's immaculate, it's been built in a short period of time," said Trump.

"And when I look at our cities, they're dirty, I must say, mostly blue [Democrat-controlled] ...and they have potholes all over the place. Railings are falling down, and everything is rusty and disgusting and the crime is through the roof."

The US leader also highlighted the energy of Shenzhen residents, which he said he had noticed after touring around the city.

Reflecting on the trilateral summit with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin, Trump said the meetings had "great electricity" and that they discussed cooperation to limit the spread of nuclear weapons. (With contributions from AFP)

articles.title: 'China, Russia, US consensus positive for HK economy'
articles.excerpt: Commerce Secretary Algernon Yau said on Saturday that the joint declaration of peace issued by President Xi Jinping and his…
articles.fullText:
Commerce Secretary Algernon Yau said on Saturday that the joint declaration of peace issued by President Xi Jinping and his Russian and US counterparts, Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump, is positive for the world economy and Hong Kong.

The three leaders released the declaration following trilateral talks on the sidelines of the Apec Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen.

Speaking on RTHK, Yau said the consensus reached by the major powers would support global stability and trade.

"In the meeting between the leaders of China, Russia and the United States, they all hoped to reach a consensus on building a peaceful world, resolving conflicts in the world and creating a prosperous global economy through cooperation," he said.

"The consensus reached by the three major countries will have an impact on the future global economy, including Hong Kong's economy."

During his keynote speech at the Apec CEO Summit, Xi said China supports establishing a world association for bay area economic cooperation to deepen exchanges between such areas and strengthen Asia-Pacific economic ties.

Yau said that as a key city in the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area, Hong Kong plays a vital role in helping the region connect with other bay areas worldwide, such as those in Japan and the United States.

The SAR can contribute, he said, by leveraging its advantages as an international centre for trade, shipping and finance.

"I think the opportunities are enormous," Yau said.

"If these bay areas can connect and boost trade, it will greatly expand import-export activity, personnel exchanges and talent complementarity."

During the Apec summit, Chief Executive John Lee also held bilateral talks with leaders from seven economies: Malaysia, Vietnam, Brunei, Thailand, Chile, Peru and Singapore.

Yau said the discussions focused on cooperation in areas such as education and trade, while also touching on tariffs and the avoidance of double taxation.

He said the chief executive also briefed the leaders about opportunities in the Northern Metropolis.

In meetings with leaders from Asean members, Lee also discussed Hong Kong's bid to join the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership, Yau added.

Edited by Robert Kemp

articles.title: Uber Parking could save you from circling the block
articles.excerpt: Uber Parking launches in 15 U.S. cities after the SpotHero deal, offering upfront prices, Uber One credits, and a future…
articles.fullText:
You finally make it downtown for dinner, but now comes the real challenge. Finding somewhere to park. You circle the block once, then again. Before you know it, you're late and getting frustrated. Sound familiar? Well, Uber thinks it has a solution. The company just launched Uber Parking, a new feature that lets you reserve a parking spot directly through the Uber app before you even leave home. Yes, the same company that built its business around getting you into someone else's car now wants to help when you drive your own. And there's another interesting twist. Uber has plans for those parking garages that involve robotaxis.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.
Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
UBER LETS PARENTS WATCH TEEN RIDES LIVE
On Nov. 9, Uber announced the launch of Uber Parking, bringing parking reservations directly into its app. The feature follows Uber's acquisition of SpotHero, a popular parking reservation service. Through that deal, Uber gained access to a network of more than 13,000 parking garages, lots and valet locations across more than 400 cities in the United States and Canada.
So, instead of driving around looking for parking, you can search for an available spot near your destination. You can also see the price upfront, making it easier to decide whether driving makes financial sense. For someone heading into the city for dinner or trying to get to an important appointment, that could save some aggravation. And if you've ever paid a small fortune to park somewhere, you'll probably appreciate being able to compare prices before arriving.
Uber has made the process pretty simple. You can book parking using the same app you already use to request a ride.
Here's how it works:
Once you've booked, your digital parking pass appears inside the Uber app. Depending on the location, you'll either scan a QR code or enter through a system that recognizes your license plate. Uber also says you can extend reservations through the app if you need more time. Cancellation policies vary by parking facility. Some reservations qualify for a full refund if canceled before the scheduled start time. Always check the booking terms before paying.
One thing worth mentioning: Uber generally won't physically park your car for you. Unless you choose a valet location, you'll still be the one behind the wheel.
FAKE E-ZPASS EMAIL THREATENS $100 FINE OVER UNPAID TOLL
Uber Parking launched in 15 U.S. cities on Nov. 9.
Those cities are:
Uber plans to expand the service into additional markets. However, there's an important detail here. Although SpotHero operates across more than 400 cities, Uber Parking has not yet expanded throughout that entire network. Also, the new feature is still rolling out. So, even if you're in one of the launch cities, you may not see the Parking icon immediately. First, make sure you're using the latest version of the Uber app. You can also visit SpotHero's website to search for parking in areas where the Uber feature is unavailable.
Here's a little bonus if you already pay for Uber One. Uber says eligible members can earn 10% back in Uber One credits on qualifying parking reservations once their parking session is complete. You can use those credits toward future eligible Uber rides or Uber Eats orders. For example, if you spend $30 on a qualifying parking reservation, you could earn $3 in Uber One credits.
That may not sound like a fortune. However, if you're regularly parking downtown, those credits could add up. Just keep in mind that the 10% reward only applies to eligible reservations. You also need an active Uber One membership to qualify and redeem the credits. And remember, these are Uber credits rather than cash back to your bank account. Before booking, compare the total parking price with other nearby options. A cheaper garage could still save you more money than the rewards you'd earn.
Uber also sees parking garages as part of its future robotaxi business . Think about it. When a driverless taxi drops someone off, what happens next? If another passenger needs a ride nearby, that's easy enough. But what happens when nobody needs the car? Does it keep driving around until another request comes in? That could mean more empty vehicles on already crowded streets. Uber is reportedly exploring ways to use parking facilities as waiting areas for autonomous vehicles. Instead of driving around without passengers, robotaxis could pull into nearby garages and wait for their next assignment.
Then, when someone requests a ride, the vehicle could head out to pick them up. Uber believes that approach could reduce unnecessary driving and help lower operating costs. There's another potential benefit. Keeping autonomous vehicles in nearby facilities could make it easier to have them ready when demand increases. However, this remains a developing plan. Uber has not announced that every SpotHero garage will accommodate robotaxis, and the company has not provided a timeline for a broad rollout of these facilities. For now, the immediate focus remains helping people find parking for their own cars.
There's something else worth paying attention to here. For years, Uber built its business around giving people an alternative to driving. Now, the company wants you opening its app even when you plan to take your own car. Let's say you're going downtown for dinner. You could check the price of an Uber ride. Then, you could compare that with the cost of driving and parking.
If driving looks cheaper, you can reserve a space through Uber. If taking a ride makes more sense, you can book that instead. Either way, Uber stays part of your plans. And as autonomous vehicles become more common, the company could eventually use that same parking network to support its robotaxi partners. It's an interesting strategy, especially as Uber looks for more ways to keep people using its app.
The biggest benefit is pretty straightforward. You may be able to reserve parking before leaving home and spend less time driving around looking for an available spot. That could be especially useful when you're heading somewhere unfamiliar or trying to make a flight. However, there are a few things I'd recommend checking before you book.
Don't assume Uber offers the lowest rate. Check the final price against other parking options before paying. Also, make sure your reservation covers the time you'll actually need.
Some parking garages have height limits. If you drive a larger SUV or truck, check those restrictions before booking. Also, confirm the exact entrance address, which may differ from the garage's street address.
Some parking reservations can be canceled for free before they begin, but the rules vary by location. Review the specific garage's cancellation terms before booking. Once your reservation starts, Uber says it can no longer be canceled or refunded.
Some garages use QR codes for entry. That's convenient, but criminals have also placed fake QR codes on parking meters to trick drivers into visiting fraudulent payment websites. Use the parking pass provided directly through your Uber app rather than scanning an unfamiliar sticker. We've previously reported on how criminals use fake parking QR codes to steal money.
Even with a reservation, finding your car afterward can still be a headache. Fortunately, Google Maps and Apple Maps have tools that can help you remember where you parked. Our guide to finding your parked car with Maps explains how to set them up.
I think Uber is onto something here. Who hasn't wasted time driving around looking for parking, especially when you're already running late? Being able to reserve a spot before leaving home sounds pretty convenient. Of course, I'd want to make sure I'm getting a good price. But what really caught my attention is Uber's plan to use parking garages for robotaxis. Having driverless cars park between rides makes sense, especially if it means fewer empty vehicles clogging up our streets. Still, I wonder what happens when those garages start filling up with robotaxis. Will there be enough room for the rest of us? That's something I'll be watching as this technology takes off.
Would you trust Uber to handle your parking reservations, or do you worry that parking garages could eventually become crowded with robotaxis, leaving fewer spaces for the rest of us? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

articles.title: Hackers use Microsoft Outlook security flaw to steal your login data
articles.excerpt: Microsoft Outlook flaw CVE-2026-124194 lets a malicious .msg file expose NTLMv2 authentication data, and Microsoft confirms hackers already exploited it.
articles.fullText:
You probably know better than to enter your password on a suspicious website. But what if hackers could steal information tied to your Windows login without ever asking for your password? That's the concern behind a Microsoft Outlook security flaw that hackers are already exploiting. Attackers can trick someone into opening a malicious Outlook file that quietly exposes Windows authentication information. That information could help a criminal impersonate you and potentially gain access to systems you use.
Microsoft released a fix on Nov. 10. However, the company confirms hackers were exploiting the vulnerability before the update became available. If you use Outlook for work, this is one security update you should check right away.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.
Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
FAKE AI EVENT INVITES TARGET MICROSOFT AND GOOGLE LOGINS
The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-124194, involves how Outlook handles specially crafted message files. An attacker can create a malicious Outlook message file, such as one using the .msg format. The hacker then needs to convince someone to open that file in an affected version of Outlook. Once opened, the malicious file can cause Outlook to connect to a server controlled by the attacker. That connection happens without the usual warning about accessing external content. During the connection, Windows can reveal NTLMv2 authentication information . This data helps Windows verify your identity when connecting to certain network services.
The information differs from your actual password. However, hackers may be able to use it in a follow-up attack to impersonate you. For someone using Outlook at work, that could potentially expose company resources their account can access. The outcome depends on the network's security protections and whether the attacker can successfully misuse the authentication information. Here's what makes this especially concerning. The attack doesn't require you to type your password into a fake login page. Opening the malicious file can be enough if your computer can connect to the attacker's network location. Microsoft says simply viewing the message through Outlook's Preview Pane does not trigger this particular vulnerability. Someone must open the malicious file for the attack to work.
Microsoft included the Outlook fix in its November Patch Tuesday security updates. The company's core release addressed 1,093 vulnerabilities, including 63 rated critical. Interestingly, Microsoft classified this particular Outlook vulnerability as moderate, giving it a CVSS severity score of 6.5 out of 10. However, that rating tells only part of the story. Microsoft confirms attackers have already exploited the flaw. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) also added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on Nov. 10. In other words, hackers are already taking advantage of this security weakness. Microsoft has not publicly identified who carried out the attacks or disclosed how many people were affected. The company also hasn't provided detailed information about the incidents. With hackers already exploiting the flaw, it's important to install the security update as soon as possible.
FAKE CHATGPT BILLING EMAILS CAN STEAL YOUR LOGIN
According to Microsoft's security advisory, the affected products include:
The vulnerability concerns affected desktop Office installations on Windows computers. Microsoft's advisory does not list Outlook.com in a web browser or the Outlook mobile apps as affected products. If your employer manages your Microsoft 365 software, your IT department may handle these updates. However, it's worth confirming that the security fix has been installed. For people who manage their own computers, here's how to check.
The most important thing you can do is update Microsoft Office. However, a few additional precautions can help reduce your exposure to suspicious files and account attacks.
Microsoft has released security updates addressing the vulnerability. You can manually check for updates in supported Windows versions of Office.
If you don't see Update Now, you may need to select Enable Updates first. If the entire Update Options menu is missing, your employer may manage updates centrally. Contact your IT department rather than assuming the software has already been patched. You can also review Microsoft's official Office update instructions.
After installing the update, you can check which version of Office is running on your computer.
For affected volume-licensed installations, Microsoft's November 10 security release includes these updated builds:
These build numbers apply to the specified LTSC editions. They shouldn't be used to check other Office versions. If you're using Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise, the correct build depends on your organization's update channel. You can check Microsoft's Office security release notes or contact your IT department to confirm the fix.
Although this vulnerability requires an Office fix, keeping Windows updated remains important.
On Windows 11:
Next, check whether Windows can receive updates for other Microsoft products.
This can help Windows deliver updates for supported Microsoft products. However, some Office installations receive updates through separate services or employer-managed systems. Remember that checking Windows Update alone may not confirm you've installed the specific Outlook fix. Check Office separately. It's also smart to back up important files before installing major operating system updates.
A message file from an unfamiliar sender deserves extra caution, especially if you weren't expecting it. Watch for attachments ending in .msg, a common file format for saved Outlook messages. The format itself is legitimate. However, attackers can abuse it to deliver this exploit. If an email claims you need to open an attached message to review an invoice or urgent workplace request, verify it through another trusted channel. Even attachments appearing to come from coworkers deserve a second look when the request seems unusual.
If something looks suspicious, avoid opening the attachment. Instead, report the message using Outlook's built-in reporting tools when available.
In supported versions of Outlook:
The exact menu location depends on your Outlook version and your employer's settings. If you're using a work account and don't see a reporting option, contact your IT department. Avoid forwarding the suspicious attachment to other coworkers.
Strong antivirus software can help identify suspicious attachments and malicious activity before they cause further damage. Look for protection that includes real-time scanning and behavior-based detection. These features may help catch threats that traditional virus signatures miss. However, antivirus software cannot replace Microsoft's security patch. Installing the Outlook update remains essential for closing this particular vulnerability. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.
Multifactor authentication (MFA) adds another layer of account protection by requiring additional verification when you sign in. Enable it on your Microsoft account and other important services whenever available. Keep in mind that MFA may not stop attacks involving stolen Windows authentication information. That's another reason updating Outlook takes priority.
If you recently opened an unexpected Outlook message attachment, don't assume everything is fine because nothing unusual appeared on your screen. Here's what to do next.
One important reminder: Changing your password alone may not address every potential exposure from this vulnerability. If you opened the attachment on a work computer, let your IT team determine whether additional security measures are necessary.
Microsoft's November security release covers far more than Outlook. It also fixes weaknesses that could allow attackers to gain additional privileges or remotely execute malicious code. For those of you using a Windows PC every day, the sheer number of vulnerabilities may sound overwhelming. However, not every flaw carries the same immediate risk. In this case, the Outlook weakness deserves your attention because Microsoft has confirmed active exploitation.
The larger concern is how easily a malicious file can take advantage of trusted software. Outlook is part of everyday communication for countless businesses, and opening saved email messages may seem harmless. This vulnerability shows why keeping Office updated deserves the same attention as updating Windows.
What concerns me about this Outlook flaw is how little someone has to do to put their information at risk. You could receive what looks like a routine work attachment, open it and unknowingly expose information that helps a hacker impersonate you. There's no obvious warning telling you something went wrong. And by the time you realize it, the damage may already be done. I also find it troubling that Microsoft rated this vulnerability moderate even though attackers were already exploiting it. Most people aren't going to spend their day reviewing security ratings, and they shouldn't have to. They need software that protects them and updates that are easy to install. My advice is simple. If you use Outlook on a Windows computer, check for Office updates today. Don't assume your computer has already taken care of it.
Should Microsoft be doing more to prevent a single malicious Outlook file from exposing your login information, or do you think keeping your software updated is enough protection? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

China raised concerns of judicial overreach after the International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, saying on Friday "such practices are not conducive" to a resolution.

"I welcome the government of Türkiye's agreement to receive 10,000 Rohingya refugees. This marks an important step in Malaysia's efforts to find a long-term solution to an issue that has long posed challenges for migration management and national security," he said.

articles.title: Former Secret Service investigator sounds alarm over AI scams as Americans grow increasingly anxious
articles.excerpt: Former Secret Service cyberfraud investigator Jason Brown warns AI voice cloning scams could trick families into losing thousands of dollars…
articles.fullText:
A former Secret Service cyberfraud investigator warned that Americans are increasingly on edge following a wave of major technology disruptions , while artificial intelligence is making scams targeting families and consumers more sophisticated.
Jason Brown, a former U.S. Secret Service cyberfraud investigator and iCounter's director of customer advisory and counter fraud lead, told Fox News Digital on Thursday that Americans have reason to be increasingly cautious about technology.
"Everybody's on edge," Brown said.
"There's been a lot of stuff that has happened in the past week in particular that people are concerned about," he continued, citing recent technology outages involving Microsoft, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and several financial institutions.
TIMELINE: AMERICA HITS A TECH WALL AS OUTAGES CRIPPLE EMAIL, GROUND FLIGHTS AND DISRUPT MAJOR BANKS
Brown acknowledged that some incidents involved infrastructure problems while others remained under investigation.
With the holiday season approaching, Brown warned that AI has made it easier for criminals to create convincing fraudulent messages , eliminating many of the warning signs consumers previously relied on.
"AI has just made the criminal a lot more efficient and a little bit more effective," Brown said.
Spelling mistakes, poor grammar and awkward phrasing — once common indicators of fraudulent messages — are becoming less reliable as criminals use AI to generate more convincing communications, he explained.
AI VOICE SCAM TRAPS MOM IN 5-HOUR KIDNAPPING NIGHTMARE
AI also allows criminals to impersonate familiar voices , potentially tricking victims into believing they are speaking with a family member in distress.
Brown described a scenario in which a scammer uses a short voice recording to impersonate someone's relative and demand thousands of dollars in gift cards.
"AI just makes them a lot more efficient and a lot less prone to errors," he said, warning that Americans must become more skeptical of suspicious messages.
"Unfortunately, we're at a point where everybody needs to have that level of distrust," he said.
As holiday shopping ramps up, Brown said scammers are likely to impersonate major delivery companies, including UPS, FedEx and the U.S. Postal Service.
FAKE E-ZPASS EMAIL THREATENS $100 FINE OVER UNPAID TOLL
He warned that fraudulent messages may claim packages cannot be delivered until additional postage is paid, with scammers demanding payment through cryptocurrency or gift cards.
"If it comes from crypto, especially if it comes from gift cards, that's a red flag for sure," Brown said.
Beyond the emotional toll, Brown warned that increasingly sophisticated scams can result in significant financial losses. He cited FBI reporting that he said identified more than 22,000 AI-related fraud cases in 2025, with losses exceeding $890 million.
Brown noted that businesses are also vulnerable to schemes in which criminals impersonate trusted vendors and redirect legitimate payments into fraudulent accounts.
AGING MEANS LEARNING HOW TO PREVENT COSTLY SCAMS TARGETING OLDER AMERICANS
The holiday season can create additional vulnerabilities as executives travel, employees take time off and temporary workers join company operations, he said.
Brown urged Americans to independently verify suspicious messages and take additional precautions when communicating with family members, including establishing a "safe word" to help confirm someone's identity during an unexpected call.
"Another thing that we always talk about with family members, set up a safe word ahead of time. Have that conversation now," he said, adding that even if a caller provides the correct word, people should still end the call and contact the person independently using a trusted number.
"The biggest safety valve for anybody in a scam when it comes over the internet via your cell phone, over the computer is stop, think and then independently verify," he added.

articles.title: PNG has the legal right to close down Taiwan’s office, but at what cost?
articles.excerpt: After Taiwan pulls out of Port Moresby, analysts weigh the pros and cons of closer ties with China.
articles.fullText:
PORT MORESBY, Papua New Guinea – The decision by Papua New Guinea to order Taiwan’s representative office in Port Moresby to close is well within the country’s legal rights, but the legal and geopolitical considerations for such a decision are distinct, a commercial lawyer based in the South Pacific country told Radio Free Asia.
In July , PNG’s Foreign Affairs Minister Justin Tkatchenko announced in an official statement the immediate cessation of operations and the formal closure of the physical presence of the Chinese Taipei Economic Office, citing Port Moresby’s recognition of Beijing.
The office served as Taiwan’s de facto diplomatic mission in PNG, facilitating trade and other exchanges despite the absence of formal diplomatic relations between the two sides.
Taiwan on Nov. 6 confirmed the office would shut down, its personnel would withdraw, and all technical missions, scholarship and training programs would cease. Taipei also announced that it would stop spot purchases of PNG’s liquefied natural gas, or LNG, Port Moresby’s largest export commodity. Prior to the closure, Taiwan had purchased about a third of PNG’s LNG exports.
Why Papua New Guinea sent Taiwan packing. (RFA Video)
The decision to force Taiwan to close its representative office is less a legal matter than a policy decision, Margareth Parua, a Port Moresby-based commercial lawyer, told RFA.
“On the information presently available, there is no clearly identified international legal obligation requiring PNG to close an unofficial Taiwanese trade office merely because it recognises the People’s Republic of China,” she said. “Given the longstanding economic and commercial relationship between PNG and Taiwan, it would be regrettable if the decision resulted in the unnecessary loss of trade, investment and other opportunities for our people.”
Weighing options
One year after PNG gained its independence from Australia in 1975, it recognized Beijing diplomatically, adopting its own version of a “One-China Policy” which closely aligns with Beijing’s “One-China Principle” that there is only one China, Taiwan is a part of China, and that the government in Beijing is the sole legal government of China. This differs from the One China Policy of the United States in that Washington’s policy merely acknowledges Beijing’s stance on Taiwan without agreeing or disagreeing with it.
Neither Port Moresby’s One-China Policy precluded unofficial relations with Taiwan, but Beijing has recently leveraged its economic might to pressure Pacific island countries in an effort to further isolate Taiwan, Jonah Bock, assistant director for research at the Alliance Futures Initiative, a Washington-based think tank, told RFA shortly after Tkatchenko’s announcement in July.
“China will continue to aggressively pursue any action that reduces Taiwan’s international space – its ethos of national rejuvenation relies on unification. It is not an option for China to stop the contest,” said Bock in July. “The move is to curry favor with the PRC and the goal is vast sums of Chinese money.”
China's President Xi Jinping (R) shakes hands with Papua New Guinea's Prime Minister James Marape before leaders take a group photo during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit in Shenzhen, in China's southern Guangdong Province, on Nov. 19, 2026.
(Greg Baker/Pool via Reuters) Parua said that PNG should carefully consider whether forcing Taipei to close its representative office was necessary to maintain its One-China Policy, and whether the benefits of doing so outweigh the costs to national interest.
The biggest risk might have been the loss of LNG sales to Taiwan, but closer ties with China can make up for that, Joseph Ealedona, a Papua New Guinean senior journalist and former media executive, told RFA.
“While we lost the gas sales, discussions are taking place for China to purchase more gas to cover for this,” he said. “It’s a positive decision given our deep relations with China and the many benefits we can take from China. China is a massive economy and we must maintain our relations with them.”
Meanwhile, PNG’s former Prime Minister Peter O’Neill commented in Port Moresby-based weekly English daily The National that the country had lost a major buyer in Taiwan, and criticized current Prime Minister James Marape saying he traded Taiwan for China and 191 million kina (US$42.2 million).
Taipei disappointed, Washington concerned, but Beijing jubilant
Taiwan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs expressed regret in its official statement on Nov. 6 announcing the closure of the representative office. The statement detailed how Taiwan had given Papua New Guinea economic, agricultural, developmental and medical support over the years.
“Regrettably, the foundation of mutual trust, established through long-term bilateral collaboration, has been seriously undermined by the recent actions of the government of Papua New Guinea,” the statement said. “The situation also reflects China’s continued use of political pressure and economic influence to interfere in the diplomatic decisions of other nations and suppress Taiwan’s international participation.”
The statement also said that the change would have a “substantial impact” on PNG’s natural gas exports.
A man walks in front of flags of Honduras, Taiwan, and other countries, displayed at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs building, in Taipei, Taiwan on March 23, 2023.
(Annabelle Chih/Reuters) A U.S. State Department spokesperson told RFA on Nov. 9 that Washington was “deeply concerned” that PNG had ordered Taipei’s office in Port Moresby closed.
“Taiwan is a reliable, likeminded, and democratic partner, and its relationships around the world provide significant benefits to the citizens of those countries, including Papua New Guinea,” the spokesperson said. “This is yet another example of Beijing’s intimidation campaign against Taiwan and its supporters around the world, which undermines the sovereign decisions of countries choosing to partner with Taiwan and threatens international peace and prosperity.”
The Chinese Embassy in Port Moresby on Nov. 10 said in a statement that the PNG government made the right decision, and criticized Taiwan’s statement as being full of “lies and empty threats.”
“We highly appreciate and applaud the PNG Government’s firm adherence to one-China principle and the concrete measures to implement this principle, which will further consolidate the political foundation for China-PNG bilateral relations and cooperation in various fields,” the statement said. “If the Taiwan side reduces its LNG imports from PNG, the loss will on its side instead of PNG side.”
Beijing also said spot purchases of PNG’s LNG would find new buyers, including China.
“As to Taiwan’s ‘assistance’ to PNG, it is almost nothing compared to the aid and assistance from China’s mainland.”
Additional reporting by Eugene Whong in Washington. Edited by Taejun Kang and Eugene Whong.

articles.title: World Court finds Myanmar responsible for Rohingya genocide in landmark ruling
articles.excerpt: Experts say the judgment marks a historic victory for the Rohingya but enforcement remains a challenge.
articles.fullText:
Updated on Nov. 19, 2026 at 11:21 a.m. ET
The International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruled on Thursday that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya, in a landmark judgment that could increase diplomatic pressure on its military-led government.
In a 9-6 decision, the United Nations’ top court found that Myanmar had violated the 1948 Genocide Convention during a military crackdown that drove more than 730,000 Rohingya to neighboring Bangladesh in 2017.
It was the first time the court had found a state responsible for committing genocide.
The judgment comes as Myanmar’s President Min Aung Hlaing, who commanded the military during the crackdown, seeks to restore his country’s international standing.
“This is a historic ruling. For the first time, the world court has found a state responsible for committing genocide – and the man who commanded those operations is now Myanmar’s president,” Richard Horsey, senior adviser for Asia at the Belgium-based International Crisis Group, said in a statement.
“The Rohingya have waited nine years to hear a court say this. It will not change their lives quickly, but it puts what was done to them on the legal record, and no amount of denial in Naypyidaw can remove it.”
UN top court rules Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya
ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa said evidence showed that Myanmar’s security forces had killed some 10,000 Rohingya during the crackdown.
“The Court finds that Myanmar’s security forces killed thousands of Rohingya ⁠civilians, perpetrated widespread acts ⁠of sexual violence as well as acts of ⁠extreme violence against children and ⁠attacked fleeing Rohingya ⁠as they sought to flee in large numbers to ‌Bangladesh,” Iwasawa said.
The court concluded that the only reasonable inference from the evidence was that Myanmar’s security forces intended to destroy a substantial part of the Rohingya population.
It also found that Myanmar had failed to fulfill its obligation to prevent genocide.
The case was brought in 2019 by The Gambia, which accused Myanmar of violating the Genocide Convention and sought to hold the Southeast Asian nation accountable for atrocities against the predominantly Muslim ethnic minority.
Myanmar has maintained that its military operations were in response to attacks on police posts by the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army, a Rohingya armed group.
Diplomatic pressure
While the judgment establishes Myanmar’s legal responsibility for genocide, questions remain over its practical consequences and whether other governments will reconsider their engagement with Naypyitaw.
“Governments rolling out the red carpet for Min Aung Hlaing will now be doing so for the head of a state found responsible for genocide. Most will carry on regardless, but it will be harder to present this as business as usual,” Horsey said.
“The court has no means of enforcing this ruling. What matters now is whether the governments engaging Naypyitaw are prepared to attach any cost to ignoring it.”
Myanmar's Union Minister for the Ministry of the President's Office Ko Ko Hlaing attends a hearing on the day the International Court of Justice delivers its judgment in the case brought by Gambia accusing Myanmar of genocide against the Rohingya Muslim minority, in The Hague, Netherlands, Nov. 19, 2026.
(Piroschka Van De Wouw/Reuters) Horsey added that the ruling was likely to make Myanmar’s government more defensive in its dealings with the United Nations as it sought to regain its seat at the world body.
Human rights advocates called on governments to use the judgment to press Myanmar to end abuses against the Rohingya.
“The International Court of Justice’s landmark ruling is long-awaited recognition of the suffering the Rohingya have endured from Myanmar’s military. The ruling also provides a significant precedent for victims of genocide, and other grave crimes, across the world in their own quest for justice,” Maria Elena Vignoli, senior international justice counsel at New York-based Human Rights Watch, said in a statement.
In response to the ruling, the United Kingdom will order the expulsion of the Myanmar defense attaché and call on the U.N. Security Council to address it, the UK’s foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, said in a statement.
“The Rohingya have endured years of appalling violence, displacement and persecution.” Miliband said. “Myanmar must comply fully with the judgement. The international community must now play its part in supporting implementation, accountability, and justice for the Rohingya.”
Uncertain future for refugees
The ruling comes amid a humanitarian crisis compounded by renewed fighting in Myanmar’s western Rakhine state, where the military has lost control of large areas to the Arakan Army, an ethnic Rakhine armed group.
“Most of the land the Rohingya fled is now held by the Arakan Army, an ethnic Rakhine armed group fighting Naypyitaw. For Rohingya still in Myanmar’s Rakhine State, how the Arakan Army treats them will matter more than anything Naypyitaw says,” Horsey said.
A Rohingya refugee gives a thumbs up while another person holds a placard following the announcement of the International Court of Justice verdict, at a refugee camp in Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh, Nov. 19, 2026.
(Mohammad Ponir Hossain/REUTERS) Nearly 1.2 million Rohingya remain in refugee camps in Bangladesh, where international aid funding cuts have led to reductions in food rations.
“Hopefully this ruling will be a reminder of their plight to donors, who need to step up,” Horsey said.
Vignoli urged the international community to ensure that the ruling translated into tangible improvements for the persecuted minority.
“Myanmar should swiftly comply with the court’s judgment and end its oppression of the Rohingya. Concerned governments should strongly support the Rohingya and promote justice for atrocities, press Myanmar’s junta to comply with the judgment, and ensure the safe and voluntary return of Rohingya refugees to Myanmar.”
Edited by Eugene Whong.
Update adds Miliband’s statement.

articles.title: P1 school results drop next Mon
articles.excerpt: Primary One discretionary places for September 2027 will be released next Monday, the Education Bureau announced today. Of the 32,104…
articles.fullText:
Primary One discretionary places for September 2027 will be released next Monday, the Education Bureau announced today.

Of the 32,104 children who applied for discretionary places at government and aided primary schools, 18,148 will be offered a place.

Among them, 8,270 have siblings studying or parents working at the schools they have applied to. The remaining 9,878 have been selected according to the Points System.

Parents who have already activated their Primary One Admission e-Platform (ePOA) account can check the results via the e-platform from 10am on Monday.

They can also bring a copy of the paper application form and check the results at the school they applied to between 9am and 5pm.

Parents whose children have been offered a discretionary place should register them next Wednesday or Thursday.

For parents whose children have failed to secure a discretionary place or who have opted for Central Allocation only, the bureau will inform them in writing in mid-January 2027 to select schools for Central Allocation via ePOA from January 18 to 24, or at a designated Central Allocation Centre on January 23 or 24.

articles.title: Trump, Xi, Putin meeting was a spectacle that yielded little progress: analysts
articles.excerpt: Leaders discussed nuclear tensions, U.S.-China rivalry over AI and Taiwan’s status, but status quo remains.
articles.fullText:
Updated on Nov. 20, 2026 at 12:48 a.m. ET
The leaders of the United States, China and Russia concluded their first-ever trilateral summit in Shenzhen on Thursday, but their meeting was more about “optics over substance,” experts told Radio Free Asia.
U.S. President Donald Trump met Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin for more than an hour on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum, describing the gathering as a historic diplomatic occasion.
Nuclear arms control and regional conflicts were high on the agenda amid deepening geopolitical and technological competition among the world’s major powers.
“As the world’s three largest nuclear powers by far, the United States, Russia and China are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth and also to lessen the risk that those weapons will ever be used,” Trump said in his opening remarks.
Although the meeting may have been historic, the three leaders have national interests that do not quite align on the nuclear question, David Fedor, a Stephenson Policy Fellow at Stanford University’s Hoover Institution, told RFA.
“Other than President Trump’s comments before the meetings about nuclear weapons, ... there was little signaling ahead of time that substantive decisions would be made,” said Fedor.
Xi called for the prohibition and destruction of nuclear weapons and the establishment of a world free of them, according to Chinese state broadcaster CCTV.
The summit marked the first leader-level talks on nuclear arms control since New START expired in February. Its lapse ended the last remaining bilateral nuclear treaty between Washington and Moscow, raising concerns about an unrestricted arms race.
Trump Xi Putin trilateral in China
Trump has called for a new agreement that would bring Beijing into nuclear arms control negotiations. China, however, has long maintained that Washington and Moscow should substantially reduce their stockpiles before asking it to accept limitations on its comparatively smaller arsenal.
China is estimated to possess more than 600 nuclear warheads, while the United States and Russia hold more than 5,000 each.
“Once you have the nuclear weapons, it’s very hard not to have them,” Trump said. “So it’s not an easy thing to do, give them up.”
Xi also proposed regular high-level exchanges and the creation of a crisis communication mechanism among the three powers to help manage tensions.
No concrete agreement on nuclear arms control was immediately announced following the summit.
The White House released a statement that said the three leaders “reaffirmed that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought.”
Russian President Vladimir Putin attends a trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Leaders' Summit in Shenzhen, China, November 19, 2026.
(Vyacheslav Prokofyev/Sputnik via Reuters) The statement also said that the three countries would hold dialogues on preventing the spread of nuclear weapons and minimizing nuclear risks.
Taiwan’s security concerns
Ahead of Thursday’s trilateral meeting, Taiwan’s government downplayed expectations that the island would feature prominently in discussions among the three leaders.
“From what we know, Taiwan is not the focus,” Mainland Affairs Council (MAC) spokesperson Liang Wen-chieh told a news briefing in Taipei.
Liang said the discussions were more likely to prioritize securing a ceasefire in Ukraine and addressing Iran’s nuclear program.
“Even if Taiwan is mentioned, it will be a relatively peripheral issue,” he said.
Liang also expressed doubts about whether the three leaders could reach substantive agreements given their competing interests and the limited time available for negotiations.
“The three parties want different things, and their priorities are also different,” he said.
Taiwan nevertheless featured in a separate bilateral meeting between Trump and Xi earlier on Thursday, their third face-to-face meeting this year.
Xi told Trump that Washington should “stick to doing the right thing” on Taiwan to avoid major setbacks in relations between the two countries, China’s official Xinhua News Agency reported.
According to Xinhua, Trump told Xi that the United States “does not support Taiwan independence.”
The White House had not released its own account of the bilateral meeting at the time of Xinhua’s report.
These statements, and others on Ukraine, seemed to be a repeat of previous statements, Ian Chong, an associate professor of political science at the National University of Singapore, told RFA.
" This whole series of meetings have been big on optics and small on deliverables," said Chong. “⁠⁠There were general declaratory statements but little visible substantive progress, at least on to the public. ... I suppose repeating the basic principles are better than nothing."
People pass a sign for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, Nov. 17, 2026.
(Pedro Pardo/AFP) During the trilateral summit, Xi also called on major powers to respect each other’s sovereignty, territorial integrity and core interests, warning against crossing red lines on sensitive issues.
Taiwan, which joined APEC in 1991 under the name Chinese Taipei, is represented at this year’s summit by Acer founder and honorary chairman Stan Shih, appointed by President Lai Ching-te to attend on his behalf.
The lack of substance in statements regarding Taiwan was likely an outcome Taipei was hoping for, William Yang, senior analyst for North East Asia at the Belgium-based International Crisis Group.
“On Taiwan, an issue where there is very little basis for bilateral consensus, they basically treated it as a formality — something they had to mention briefly as part of the routine agenda, and then move on,” said Yang. “I think, overall, when the two sides’ readouts came out yesterday, the immediate reaction from the Taiwan government was probably one of relief.”
Neither Xi’s nor Trump’s statement did much to change the status quo for Taiwan, he said.
“Basically, Taiwan made it through another Trump-Xi meeting without any rhetoric being put forward that would cause major harm to Taiwan.”
Competition over artificial intelligence
The summit took place against a backdrop of mounting technological rivalry between Washington and Beijing, particularly over artificial intelligence (AI) and access to advanced semiconductors.
Trump has held off on imposing tougher restrictions on China’s access to advanced chips used to develop AI models, indicating that additional measures could aggravate bilateral tensions.
Xi urged Washington and Moscow to work with Beijing to maintain stable global supply chains and called on the three powers to “abandon Cold War mentality, not pursue decoupling and breaking chains.”
Competition over emerging technologies has become a major point of friction between the world’s two largest economies, alongside disagreements over trade and access to strategically important raw materials.
China's President Xi Jinping, U.S. President Donald Trump and Russia's President Vladimir Putin arrive for a trilateral meeting at Kylin Villa on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, Nov. 19, 2026.
(Doug Mills/AFP) U.S. officials have accused Beijing of failing to fully implement commitments made during a Trump-Xi meeting last year, including pledges to purchase more American agricultural products and ease export restrictions on rare earth minerals used in electronics manufacturing.
A trade truce reached last year following successive tariff increases is due to expire on Jan. 10, 2027, adding another source of uncertainty to bilateral relations.
The meeting between Xi and Trump did little to ease this uncertainty, Riley Walters, deputy director of the Japan Chair at the Washington-based Hudson Institute, told RFA.
“It sounds like Trump and U.S. officials are still waiting on China to buy more soybeans and export more rocks, meaning maybe no progress is being made since their last meeting,” said Riley.
“Instead, it sounds like Trump and Xi simply meeting and talking has become the baseline for this relationship, and so long as they continue meeting then it’s construction.”
Fedor said that Trump seems to feel a sense of responsibility in managing relationships with Xi and Putin.
That sentiment is what drives him to ”stage these very public interactions with leaders like Chairman Xi and President Putin," he said.
“But I do not think those visits substantively change the underlying interests of the relevant parties, at least some of which are fundamentally contradictory.”
Edited by Eugene Whong.
Update adds comments from experts.

articles.title: Could caviar served on gourmet food tour of North Korea violate UN sanctions?
articles.excerpt: Russian tour company offers a tour of high-end Pyongyang restaurants inaccessible to average North Koreans.
articles.fullText:
Read a version of this story in Korean .
Caviar, wine, and foie gras served to Russian tourists in high-end Pyongyang restaurants is not necessarily evidence that exporters are violating sanctions that prohibit luxury items shipments to North Korea, but in the spirit of the sanctions these should be considered luxury items, a former member of the U.N. sanctions committee told Radio Free Asia.
Russian travel agency Vostok Intur is offering a gourmet tour that includes meals at many of the places frequented by North Korean elites: the twin-tower Koryo Hotel; the iconic Okryu-gwan restaurant, ground zero for Pyongyang’s high-class food culture; and a cruise ship sailing down the Taedong River which runs through the city.
The Russian Union of Travel Industry reported Monday that the travel company had completed its first gourmet tour with each participant paying roughly US$2,000 for the experience. The tour package includes an itinerary visiting restaurants inaccessible on standard tours, Inna Mukhina, the director of the travel agency, said in the report. The tour route and the restaurants are approved by North Korean tourism authorities, and it includes a stop at a restaurant called Rungra, where caviar and foie gras is served.
A table setting at a high-end Pyongyang restaurant, released by Vostok Intour, a travel agency based in Vladivostok, Russia.
(Vostok Intur) But whether this is a violation of sanctions depends on the interpretation of U.N. resolution 1718 – adopted by the U.N. Security Council in 2006 as a means to prevent the flow of cash and resources into North Korea’s nuclear missile programs. The resolution lists 14 luxury items that are banned for sale to North Korea, but caviar and foie gras are not among them.
The sanctions document should be viewed broadly rather than narrowly, Shuji Sue, a former member of the U.N. Panel of Experts on North Korea sanctions, told RFA Tuesday.
“Because the luxury goods are not specifically exemplified, this has always been a subject of debate when the panel of experts drafts reports,” he said. “I reiterate that I view caviar as a luxury item and consider it to be a luxury product prohibited by the Security Council.”
The European Union designates caviar and its substitutes as prohibited luxury goods, and the U.K., Japan, and Singapore also ban the export of caviar to North Korea. Wine is also subject to the luxury goods export ban by the E.U., the U.S., and the U.K.
Vostok Intur plans to regularize gourmet tourism starting in 2027, once a month with a maximum of 10 people per trip. According to the itinerary released on the agency’s website, tourists will visit the Koryo Hotel restaurant, the Hwasong Kumgang restaurant at the top of the Pyongyang Clock Tower, the Taedong River floating restaurant, and Okryu-gwan.
The price of next year’s group tour package announced by the travel agency is approximately US$1,100, which includes a basic cost of 45,000 rubles (about US$550) plus US$550 for local accommodation expenses. Meal costs are calculated separately.
Even if the sanctions resolution is interpreted broadly, the caviar would not be a violation if it were produced domestically. RFA asked Vostok Intur about the source of the ingredients, but they did not respond.
Domestic production?
Though the source of the caviar has not been confirmed, North Korea has been farming sturgeon since the reign of Kim Jong Il, the father and predecessor of current leader Kim Jong Un. The state-run Korean Central News Agency reported in 2013 that the younger Kim visited a fish farm in South Hwanghae province, and said that his father’s last order before he died in 2011 was to raise as many sturgeon as possible so they could be prepared and served at Okryu-gwan.
This undated picture released by North Korea's official Korean Central News Agency on Feb. 21, 2017 shows North Korean leader Kim Jong-Un visiting the Samchon catfish farm in South Hwanghae Province, North Korea.
(KCNA via AFP) RFA was not able to confirm whether North Korea produces caviar domestically, but if it does, it can only be in small quantities, Lee Hyunseung, a former member of the North Korean elite whose family fled North Korea in 2014 and who now resides in the United States, told RFA.
“We cannot confirm the exact production volume, but as long as fish farms exist, domestic production is possible,” said Lee, who works as a senior researcher at the Maryland-based Global Peace Foundation. “However, mass production is not feasible. Clearly, if the number of tourists increases and tourism programs are operated more frequently, imports would be necessary to guarantee the required quantity.”
China is the world’s largest producer and exporter of sturgeon caviar but Beijing’s official export statistics show no record of the delicacy being sent to North Korea between 2018 and 2025. Russia, meanwhile, has not disclosed bilateral trade statistics since 2022, meaning that potentially Chinese caviar could enter North Korea via Russia.
Inequality exposed
The gourmet food tours are a stark contrast to the lifestyles of the typical resident of North Korea, a country that struggles with chronic food shortages, where a month’s salary cannot even buy a bag of rice.
Lee said that restaurants such as the Koryo Hotel or the Taedong River cruise ship can cost up to hundreds of dollars for a single meal, making them inaccessible to most people living in North Korea.
RFA reported last month that an average factory worker earns 20,000 North Korean won, about 30 US cents at the market exchange rate.
According to Vostok Intur’s itineraries, the tourists’ lunches and dinners are ordered and paid for separately, with an average cost of US$20 per meal. This amount is equivalent to approximately five and a half times the average worker’s annual salary.
A group of Russian tourists arrive at the Pyongyang International Airport in Pyongyang, North Korea, Friday, Feb. 9, 2024.
(Cha Song Ho/AP) “ Russians travel to North Korea like this, pay US$2,000, and enjoy a luxurious trip for three nights and four days,” said Lee. “I wonder how many people in North Korea can actually afford to pay US$2,000 and enjoy that kind of luxury. Even the wealthy elites in the country simply cannot spend like that.”
According to South Korea’s Ministry of Unification, the cash-strapped North Korean government regards tourism as a key means of earning badly needed foreign currency.
“These tourism profits will also eventually be handed over to Kim Jong Un through the General Administration of National Tourism,” said Lee.
Edited by Yi Yongin in Korean and Eugene Whong in English.

articles.title: Rohingya hope for justice as UN court prepares to rule on Myanmar genocide case
articles.excerpt: An activist who fled Myanmar’s 2017 military crackdown says a historic ruling must lead to real change for refugees
articles.fullText:
A Rohingya activist who fled Myanmar as a teenager hopes a landmark ruling by the United Nations’ highest court on Thursday will bring long-awaited recognition of her community’s suffering, she told Radio Free Asia.
The International Court of Justice (ICJ) in The Hague is set to rule Nov. 19 on whether Myanmar violated the 1948 Genocide Convention during a military crackdown against the predominantly Muslim Rohingya minority in 2017, which forced more than 730,000 people to flee to neighboring Bangladesh.
Though she hopes for a favorable ruling, Lucky Karim, a Rohingya who escaped the violence at the age of 14 and is now a human rights activist, warned that justice will mean little without action to protect refugees and allow them to return home.
“For Rohingya to have a positive outcome, it will be a historic moment, a historic victory for us,” she told RFA, adding that such a ruling could also offer hope to other ethnic minority communities in Myanmar, where years of conflict and military repression have displaced millions of people.
Lucky Karim, in front row on the left, with classmates at a primary school in Hlaing Thi village, Maungdaw Township, Rakhine State.
(Lucky Karim) Originally from Hlaing Thi village in Rakhine State’s Maungdaw township, Karim spent six years in a refugee camp in Bangladesh. In 2022, she founded Refugee Women for Peace and Justice, an organization advocating for the rights and education of Rohingya women.
Her hopes reflect the significance of a case that has taken seven years to reach a judgment and could establish Myanmar’s legal responsibility for one of the worst episodes of mass displacement in recent decades.
What happened to the Rohingya?
The Rohingya are a predominantly Muslim ethnic minority from Myanmar’s western Rakhine State who have faced decades of discrimination, restrictions on movement and denial of citizenship in the Buddhist-majority country.
In August 2017, Myanmar’s military launched what it described as clearance operations after Rohingya militants attacked security posts. Soldiers were accused of killing civilians, raping women and burning entire villages, driving hundreds of thousands of people across the border into Bangladesh.
A United Nations fact-finding mission later concluded that there were reasonable grounds to infer genocidal intent behind the military campaign and called for senior military officials to be investigated and prosecuted.
Myanmar has rejected accusations of genocide, maintaining that its operations were legitimate responses to attacks by the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army, a Rohingya insurgent group.
The Gambia, a small West African nation, brought the case against Myanmar in November 2019 with the backing of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation.
It accused Myanmar of violating the Genocide Convention, an international treaty adopted after World War II that obliges countries to prevent and punish genocide.
A view of the Great Hall of Justice, the courtroom of the International Court of Justice (ICJ), at the Peace Palace in The Hague, Netherlands, June 18, 2026. (Nicolas Economou/Reuters)
(Reuters) The ICJ ordered Myanmar in January 2020 to take measures to prevent genocidal acts against the Rohingya and preserve evidence.
Myanmar’s government filed objections to the case in January 2021, just days before the country’s military took control of the country in a coup.
The court rejected the objections in 2022, and held hearings on the allegations in January this year.
During those hearings, The Gambia argued that the pattern of killings, sexual violence and destruction demonstrated an intent to destroy the Rohingya as a group. Myanmar’s military government disputed that interpretation, arguing that the evidence did not meet the legal threshold required to establish genocide.
What could the ruling change?
Thursday’s judgment will determine whether Myanmar bears responsibility under international law for violations of the Genocide Convention.
Unlike the International Criminal Court, which prosecutes individuals, the ICJ settles disputes between countries. Its ruling cannot directly send military commanders to prison or compel the immediate return of refugees.
But a finding against Myanmar would carry legal and diplomatic weight and could require the country to take further measures to address violations and provide reparations.
For Karim, the distinction between a legal victory and improvements in refugees’ lives is crucial.
“The judgment from the International Court of Justice does not immediately change the ground reality. It doesn’t immediately repatriate refugees from refugee camps to Burma either,” she said, using Myanmar’s former name.
The challenges facing the Rohingya have only deepened since the 2017 crackdown.
After the 2021 coup, the country was plunged into a wider civil war. Renewed fighting in Rakhine State between the military and the Arakan Army, an ethnic Rakhine armed group, has exposed Rohingya civilians to further violence and displacement.
The United Nations said in May that approximately 150,000 Rohingya had arrived in Bangladesh since early 2024, adding to the pressure on already overcrowded refugee settlements.
Around 1.2 million Rohingya refugees were living in Bangladesh, according to the UN’s May estimate, most of them in and around Cox’s Bazar, home to one of the world’s largest refugee settlements.
Their return to Myanmar remains fraught with uncertainty, with concerns over safety, citizenship rights and protection from persecution still unresolved.
Lucky Karim is seen in front of the house where he lived in refugee camp number 8 in Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh, in March 2019.
(Lucky Karim) “Until it is safe for everyone, it’s not safe for any one of us in Burma,” Karim said.
She urged governments and international organizations to ensure that any judgment leads to concrete measures to protect refugees and create conditions for their safe, voluntary and dignified return.
The ICJ’s judgments are legally binding, although the court has no independent enforcement force. If a country fails to comply, the other party may seek action through the UN Security Council.
Karim said achieving lasting change would require sustained international commitment and the implementation of the court’s ruling, rather than simply recognizing the atrocities committed against the Rohingya.
“So the judgment should not be a piece of paper,” she said. “It shouldn’t be another genocide declaration.”
Edited by Eugene Whong.

articles.title: Trump-Xi-Putin summit puts nuclear arms control, North Korea in focus
articles.excerpt: Analysts see little prospect of a nuclear deal, while Pyongyang hopes its allies will press its case with the US.
articles.fullText:
When U.S. President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin hold their first trilateral summit on Thursday in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the APEC summit , a concrete agreement on nuclear arms control would be an unlikely result, analysts told Radio Free Asia.
The meeting comes as Washington seeks to bring Beijing into nuclear discussions with Moscow, while China maintains that its smaller arsenal makes participation in such negotiations unreasonable. North Korea, meanwhile, is closely monitoring the meeting for any implications it might have for its own nuclear weapons program.
Though a deal is not likely, the summit could open channels for further consultations on nuclear risks, Cheng Xiaonong, a U.S.-based Chinese scholar, told RFA Mandarin.
“My understanding is that Trump is essentially trying to use Putin to teach Xi Jinping a lesson,” he said. “Of course, Putin will want to negotiate something in return.”
U.S. President Donald Trump shakes hands with Russian President Vladimir Putin as China’s President Xi Jinping stands beside, before the welcome banquet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, Nov. 18, 2026.
(Iori Sagisawa/Reuters) Trump is scheduled to meet Xi bilaterally before joining Putin for trilateral talks. Discussions are expected to include nuclear disarmament or the wars in Ukraine and Iran, although China has not released a detailed agenda.
North Korea, which maintains close ties with both Beijing and Moscow, has not publicly commented on the summit, but analysts say Pyongyang may hope its allies will use the meeting to advance its longstanding demands for recognition as a nuclear-armed state and relief from international sanctions.
Competing nuclear interests
The United States and Russia have decades of experience negotiating nuclear arms control agreements, but China has resisted joining similar negotiations, arguing that its nuclear arsenal remains substantially smaller.
Cheng said that China’s continued nuclear expansion and reliance on strategic deterrence would make a trilateral agreement difficult.
He said Washington would seek a commitment from Xi to restrain China’s nuclear arsenal, while Beijing and Moscow would pursue their own objectives in negotiations with Trump.
“All three have their own calculations, and they can’t work together,” Cheng said. “Under those circumstances, a joint statement would be meaningless.”
Spectators wave Chinese flags as military vehicles carrying DF-41 nuclear ballistic missiles roll during a parade to commemorate the 70th anniversary of the founding of Communist China in Beijing, Oct. 1, 2019.
(Mark Schiefelbein/AP) Xi will likely use the summit to demonstrate China’s status as a major power and strengthen his domestic political authority, Song Guocheng, a Taiwanese international relations scholar, told RFA Mandarin.
He also considered a concrete nuclear arms control agreement unlikely but said the leaders could still make progress on reducing nuclear risks.
The leaders “could establish what we call a nuclear weapons communication mechanism, with emergency procedures or arrangements between them,” Song said. “That could at least help prevent nuclear miscalculations.”
China’s Foreign Ministry said Monday that the leaders would exchange views on maintaining world peace and promoting strategic stability among major powers.
Beijing has previously said requiring China to participate in trilateral nuclear disarmament negotiations at this stage would be neither reasonable nor realistic.
North Korea seeks recognition, fears concessions
For North Korea, analysts say the summit could provide an opportunity to seek diplomatic support for its nuclear ambitions, although Pyongyang is not participating in the talks.
North Korea likely hopes that China and Russia will convey Pyongyang’s demands to Trump, Kim Tae-woo, a former president of the Seoul-based Korea Institute for National Unification, told RFA Korean.
“North Korea essentially has two demands and expectations when it comes to nuclear weapons,” Kim said. “The first is recognition of its status as a nuclear-armed state. The second is that any nuclear talks with the United States must be conducted as arms reduction negotiations between nuclear powers on an equal footing.”
Analysts said an explicit endorsement of North Korea’s nuclear status was unlikely, but the absence of calls for denuclearization could still be welcomed by Pyongyang.
This image distributed by the North Korean government on March 24, 2022, and not independently verifiable shows leader Kim Jong Un walking away from what state media reports as a "new type" of intercontinental ballistic missile.
(KCNA via Reuters) “North Korea will hope that there are no statements about stability on the Korean Peninsula or North Korea’s denuclearization,” Shin Beom-chul, South Korea’s former vice minister of national defense, told RFA Korean. “They will be satisfied as long as denuclearization is not discussed.”
North Korea may also hope Beijing and Moscow will press Washington to ease sanctions, analysts said.
In December 2017, the U.N. Security Council – which includes Russia and China – adopted Resolution 2397, which imposed tighter restrictions on North Korea’s petroleum supplies, exports and overseas workers.
The summit could present risks for Pyongyang if China or Russia uses their relationships with North Korea as leverage.
Recent high-level diplomatic exchanges between North Korea and its neighbors might be showing Pyongyang’s concerns about being sidelined, Ko Young-hwan, a former president of South Korea’s National Institute for Unification Education, told RFA Korean.
“The war in Ukraine won’t go on forever,” Ko said. “North Korea is probably worried that China and Russia might do something with the United States behind its back.”
South Korea’s presidential office has said Seoul’s position and interests must be fully reflected in discussions among the three powers.
Prospects for further talks
Beyond nuclear arms control, analysts differ on whether the summit could lead to a more permanent diplomatic framework among Washington, Beijing and Moscow.
A scholar of U.S.-China relations identified only as Mr. Xing told RFA Mandarin that the meeting could signal the emergence of a “new Yalta system,” referring to the 1945 conference at which Allied leaders discussed the postwar international order.
Members of the "Art Lift" collective carry the artwork showing U.S. President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping next to the 'Big Three' monument with the leaders at the 1945 Yalta conference - Joseph Stalin, Franklin D. Roosevelt and Winston Churchill, in Livadia park in Yalta, Crimea, Nov. 16, 2026.
(Alexey Pavlishak/Reuters) Xing predicted the summit would remain largely symbolic, with China unlikely to support a formal consultation mechanism.
The U.S.-based Arms Control Association said ahead of the meeting that a single summit was unlikely to produce a major breakthrough, but the leaders could instruct negotiating teams to begin sustained discussions on nuclear arms limits and risk reduction.
The Kremlin said the parties were discussing a possible joint communiqué. If they cannot agree on a text, the three leaders will issue separate assessments of the talks.
Edited by Taejun Kang and Eugene Whong.

articles.title: Govt to fund sub-degree progs
articles.excerpt: The Education Bureau announced today that the Study Subsidy Scheme for Designated Professions/Sectors will subsidise 2,196 places in 35 sub-degree…
articles.fullText:
The Education Bureau announced today that the Study Subsidy Scheme for Designated Professions/Sectors will subsidise 2,196 places in 35 sub-degree programmes at five post-secondary institutions for the 2027/28 academic year.

The programmes span seven disciplines facing strong manpower demand: architecture and engineering, computer science, creative industries, healthcare, sports and recreation, testing and certification, and tourism and hospitality.

Annual subsidies for the 2027/28 academic year will be $40,730 for laboratory-based programmes and $23,390 for non-laboratory-based programmes.

The subsidy applies to both new and continuing eligible students and covers the normal duration of the programmes.

Students in need may still apply for assistance from the Student Finance Office under the Working Family & Student Financial Assistance Agency to help cover the remaining tuition fees payable.

articles.title: Smiles and hugs ahead of Trump, Xi and Putin’s highly anticipated meeting
articles.excerpt: Shenzhen – China’s tech capital – rolls out the red carpet for the 33rd APEC summit.
articles.fullText:
SHENZHEN, China – U.S. President Donald Trump was greeted by Chinese President Xi Jinping at the bottom of the stairs of Air Force One upon landing in China on Wednesday for this week’s APEC summit.
Trump, Xi, Putin at APEC in Shenzhen
Both leaders embraced on the red carpet at Shenzhen Bao’an International Airport as a crowd of women waved American flags and chanted “warm welcome” in Mandarin. Trump had just flown in from Manila where he had attended the ASEAN summit. The scene echoed Trump’s welcome at Joint Base Andrews at the start of Xi’s state visit to the United States in September.
Chinese President Xi Jinping welcomes U.S. President Donald Trump as he arrives at Shenzhen Airport to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Leaders Summit in Shenzhen, China Nov. 18, 2026.
(Carlos Barria/Reuters) Shenzhen is hosting leaders from 21 Asia-Pacific economies during the two-day summit, but the scheduled meeting between Trump, Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday is the highly anticipated event.
The planned talks – to be held at Shenzhen’s lakeside Kylin Villa – echo the February 1945 summit of Britain’s Winston Churchill, the Soviet Union’s Joseph Stalin and U.S. President Franklin Delano Roosevelt in Yalta, months before the end of World War II.
“He will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous,” Olivia Wales, a White House spokeswoman, said on a call with reporters about the meeting last week.
Trump later arrived at the venue of the APEC dinner, pausing to enjoy a rendition of “America the Beautiful” by a Chinese string and woodwind ensemble before being greeted by Xi and Chinese First Lady Peng Liyuan.
Servers prepare for a welcome banquet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Economic Leaders' Meeting at the Shenzhen International Communication Center in Shenzhen, China, Nov. 18, 2026.
(Maxim Shemetov/AFP) As leaders gathered for the APEC family photo ahead of the dinner, a smiling Putin walked up to Trump and extended his hand as Xi looked on.
At the dinner, Xi took the stage and offered a toast to the “shared prosperity” of the Asia-Pacific region.
Shenzhen sparkles
As host city to the 33rd meeting of APEC economic leaders, China’s tech capital was on full display Wednesday. Promotional signage adorned the airport, many buildings and roadways. Flags decorated the trees and lampposts, giving the entire city a festive atmosphere.
A woman walks past a decorative sign for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, Nov. 16, 2026.
(Pedro Pardo/AFP) The streets were pristine, with everything meticulously organized, as if the city was eager to showcase its rapid development.
At the same time, police were stationed throughout the city to control traffic and ensure security. A heavy police presence was also evident around the International Media Center, where journalists from across the globe had gathered.
To enter the center, journalists passed through security checkpoints and were subject to rigorous screening; their photographs automatically appeared on a screen as they underwent baggage inspections and body searches, reflecting a strict emphasis on security protocols.
Security agents guard the hotel where U.S. President Donald Trump will stay during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, Nov 18, 2026.
(Pedro Pardo/AFP) Amid these measures, numerous volunteers were stationed on the shuttle buses connecting hotels to the media center, as well as inside the hotels and the media center itself, to assist journalists and other attendees.
The two-day summit ends Thursday, after which Trump is scheduled to immediately return to the U.S.
Edited by Eugene Whong.

articles.title: South China Sea code of conduct could depend on landlocked Laos: analysts
articles.excerpt: ASEAN meetings again ended without a code of conduct, and Vientiane might have influence in future negotiations.
articles.fullText:
Landlocked Laos could play a huge role in future negotiations between ASEAN and China on a South China Sea code of conduct, potentially tipping the scales for Beijing, but close ties with its northern neighbor do not mean that Vientiane is acting as a proxy to block negotiations, analysts told Radio Free Asia.
As the leaders of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, or ASEAN, concluded their summit in Manila this week, the bloc again failed to finalize the code of conduct, or COC – an agreement that would seek to prevent confrontations in the sea which is claimed in its entirety by China and in part by Vietnam, the Philippines, Brunei and Malaysia.
The COC has been in negotiations for decades, and hammering out the agreement during this week’s meeting was a priority for the bloc’s current chair, the Philippines, a country with an exclusive economic zone, or EEZ, that significantly overlaps the territory claimed by China within its nine-dash line. Philippines foreign minister Ma. Theresa Lazaro on Nov. 15 told reporters that about 80% of a draft of the code had been completed.
But the agreement will have to wait until at least next year, when the next ASEAN meeting will be held in Singapore.
The overlapping claims of China and the Philippines in the South China Sea.
(AFP) Laos as an ASEAN member state wields significant influence despite not having any claims in the South China Sea, as the bloc operates on a consensus system.
